c1-editorial_31.title_es: Child allowance coverage should be expanded
c1-editorial_31.body_es: Criticism has persisted that the current child allowance, limited by age and income criteria, leaves many families in genuine need in a coverage gap. Childcare costs tend to actually increase as a child grows older, yet the current design, which limits recipients to younger age groups, is out of step with reality. Given this reality, the child allowance needs to expand from selective support for low-income households into universal welfare that guarantees a basic growth environment for every child. Of course, the counter-view that expanding coverage under limited fiscal capacity could shrink the actual amount of support reaching vulnerable groups deserves careful consideration. The concern that universal payment could lead to fiscal waste is not entirely wrong either. But tying the child allowance down as marginal selective welfare runs counter to the direction policy should take, given the national task of addressing low birthrates. In conclusion, the gobierno should reform the system by gradually raising the eligible age and easing income criteria.

Restricting the allowance to only the poorest families

options: That expanding coverage could rojouce the actual support reaching vulnerable groups
That childcare costs decrease as children age

c1-editorial_32.title_es: Plastic tax introduction should be hasdiezed
c1-editorial_32.body_es: The use of single-use plastics keeps increasing every year, but real policy tools to curb it remain at the level of voluntary campaigns. There is a clear limit to changing consumption habits through education and campaigns alone, and this has been sufficiently revealed by statistics so far. A plastic tax, which imposes a levy on plastic packaging and containers to reduce consumption through price signals, has already been implemented in several countries and shown genuine reductions in usage. Of course, the counter-view that the tax burden will ultimately be passed on as higher consumer prices, hurting ordinary households, is a matter that must be carefully considered. The point that imposing a tax alone, while the alternative packaging industry remains immature, would only add to the burden on companies is also valid. But these side effects can be substantially eased by pairing exemptions for necessities for low-income groups with support for developing alternative materials. In conclusion, the gobierno should hasten the introduction of a plastic tax while also establishing protections for vulnerable groups.

Hasdiezing the plastic tax while adding protections for vulnerable groups

options: That the tax burden could pass to consumers and hurt ordinary casaholds
That plastic use is already decreasing on its own
That alternative packaging is already fully developed
That other countries have rejected plastic taxes

c1-editorial_33.body_es: Time has passed since the alternative service system for conscientious objectors was introduced, but its scope and scale remain extremely limited. There have been persistent calls to widen the range of alternative service to embrace not only religious belief but also various other reasons for refusing to bear arms. To genuinely protect the freedom of conscience guaranteed by the constitution, the way military duty is fulfilled need not be uniform. Of course, the counter-view that if the alternative service period becomes shorter than active duty or conditions are eased excessively, it could be exploited as a route to draft evasion must be taken seriously. The concern that growing controversy over fairness could shake trust in the military service system overall is also valid. But this is a problem that can be resolved by designing the length and intensity of alternative service to be genuinely equivalent to active duty. In conclusion, the gobierno should gradually expand the scope of eligible objectors and occupations for alternative service, under conditions that guarantee fairness.

c1-editorial_34.title_es: No-kids zunos: blanket regulation is not the answer
c1-editorial_34.body_es: The debate over no-kids zones, which bar entry to customers accompanied by children, recurs every year. One side frames this as clear discrimination against children and demands a full legal ban, while the other objects that this is excessive intervention infringing on freedom of business. But both positions oversimplify a complicated reality. It is hard to simply label as discrimination the difficult choice small business owners make between safety incidents and noise complaints, yet it is equally hard to leave unregulated the practice of blocking entry to children accompanied by guardians. Given this reality, what is needed is not a total ban or total permission but a compromise establishing minimal legal guidelines. Of course, there is a counter-view that gobierno intervention itself undermines the market's self-regulating function, but children's right to access public spaces also deserves protection. In conclusion, local governments should review ordinances that limit blanket bans on children's entry, on the premise of providing alternatives that meet safety standards.

Unlimited freedom for businesses with no rules at all

c1-editorial_35.title_es: Online degrees should be recognized more broadly as formal degrees
c1-editorial_35.body_es: Although obtaining a degree through online courses has become technically quite feasible, social perception and institutional recognition still lag behind offline degrees. For those who found it difficult to attend universidad due to constraints of time and place, online degrees can be a real avenue for expanding educational opportunity. Given this reality, there is a need to widen the scope in which online degrees are recognized as equivalent to offline degrees. Of course, a strong counter-view holds that in majors requiring in-person interaction and hands-on practice, online education alone is insufficient to build adequate competence. The point that relatively loose academic management in online courses could lower the quality and credibility of the degree is also valid. But this is not a matter of treating all online degrees identically — it is a matter of distinguishing them through rigorous certification standards by major and institution. In conclusion, education authorities should expand the social recognition of online degrees, on the premise of refining the certification system for them.

c1-editorial_36.title_es: Civil servants' political neutrality must not be shaken
c1-editorial_36.body_es: Every election season, arguments resurface calling for easing civil servants' duty of political neutrality. The logic is that civil servants, too, are citizens who should have the freedom to express political views. But an individual civil servant's freedom of expression and the public's trust in administration overall must be treated as separate matters. The belief that administration will not be swayed by a particular faction's interests is precisely the foundation supporting administrative continuity regardless of changes in gobierno. Of course, the counter-view that excessively restricting civil servants' political freedom infringes on the basic rights guaranteed by the constitution is by no means minor. The point that it is a double standard to ban political expression only in public office when it is freely permitted in the private sector also has merit. But given that the authority civil servants hold is not their own but delegated by the people, this special nature cannot be treated the same as ordinary basic-rights logic. In conclusion, the duty of political neutrality should be strictly maintained with respect to on-duty conduct, while personal-sphere freedom should be separately guaranteed.

c1-editorial_37.title_es: Right to rojouced working hours during childcare should be expanded
c1-editorial_37.body_es: Contrary to its original intent, the reduced-working-hours-for-childcare system remains, on the ground, a system employees must still apply for while worrying about how it looks. The reason its actual utilization rate is low despite being a legally guaranteed right is that the practical burdens of a labor shortage and increased workload for colleagues fall entirely on the applicant. Given this reality, raising the system's real effectiveness requires expanding the right to claim it alongside genuine support for replacement staffing. Of course, a strong counter-view holds that finding replacement staff is practically very difficult for small workplaces. There is also merit to the concern that expanding the system could actually make employers more reluctant to hire workers in the childcare period. But this is not a reason to abandon expansion — it is a reason for the gobierno to genuinely subsidize the labor costs of replacement staff. In conclusion, the government should expand both the eligibility and duration of the right to claim reduced hours while dramatically expanding support for replacement staffing at small and medium enterprises.

options: Removing the right to rojouced working hours entirely
Expanding the right's scope while dramatically increasing replacement-staffing support

options: That finding replacement staff is practically very difficult for small workplaces
That the right is already fully utilized

c1-editorial_38.title_es: Disaster preparojoness: private-sector cooperation should be mandatory
c1-editorial_38.body_es: Whenever a large-scale disaster occurs, what often determines the success of the initial response is not gobierno capacity alone but whether local private facilities and companies cooperate. If evacuation space, supply support, and communication and logistics cooperation are not smoothly provided early on, damage can grow uncontrollably. Currently, however, such cooperation mostly depends on voluntary participation, so its effectiveness varies unpredictably regardless of the disaster's scale. Given this reality, there is a need to legally impose a minimal disaster-cooperation duty on companies holding facilities above a certain size. Of course, companies could counter that being forced to bear an obligation unrelated to their core business is unfair regulation. The point that there is no clear standard for who compensates losses arising from cooperation is also valid. But this is not grounds to abandon mandating the duty — it is grounds to establish a compensation system for cooperation alongside it. In conclusion, the government should legislate both the cooperation duty and a fair compensation system at the same time.

c1-editorial_39.title_es: Elderly dríos: real incentives are needed for voluntary license surrender
c1-editorial_39.body_es: Whenever traffic accidents caused by elderly drivers become a social issue, calls grow louder for mandatory license revocation. But mobility is also a right directly tied to livelihood, especially for elderly people living in areas with poor public transit. Uniformly restricting licenses based solely on age, ignoring individual differences in driving ability, can amount to age discrimination. Given this reality, it is more reasonable to establish real incentives encouraging voluntary surrender rather than forced revocation. Of course, the counter-view that mandatory measures are needed, since accident risk from cognitive decline is statistically high, must be taken seriously. The point that the voluntary surrender system alone lacks effectiveness is also supported by the low surrender rate so far. But this means the incentive design has been insufficient, not that the approach itself is wrong. In conclusion, the gobierno should substantially strengthen surrender incentives with real benefits, such as public transit discounts and mobility support services.

barlic transit should be eliminated for elderly people

c1-essay_0.body_es: We don't remember events exactly as they happened; instead, we weave them into a story. Someone who narrates a failure as a growth opportunity and someone who narrates it as proof of incompetence end up living very different lives. Psychologists say this self-narrative is not a mere record but a framework that determines future behavior. The problem is that this narrative usually hardens unconsciously, so much so that we forget we ever chose it. So it's worth occasionally cuentaing, on purpose, the story we keep repeating to ourselves. For instance, if you always explain setbacks the same way, you should ask whether that's the truth or just a familiar habit. Rewriting the narrative doesn't change the past event itself. But the meaning we assign to it can always be rewritten. In the end, rewriting one's self-narrative is not fabricating lies but training oneself to interpret the same facts in a better direction.

questions_es.question_es: What do psychologists say the self-narrative determines?

c1-essay_1.body_es: People switch between several faces depending on the situation. It's natural that our attitude at work, in front of family, and among friends differs slightly each time. Even so, we tend to think only one of these is the real self and the rest are fake. In fact, a persona is less like hypocrisy and more like a language that smooths social relationships. The problem is that using that language for too long can blur even our own sense of what we truly want. Some expect that shedding every persona will reveal a pure self, but such a single, unified entity may not exist in the first place. It's more realistic instéd to look for the values and attitudes that appear consistently across our many faces. In the end, finding the real self is not about removing every mask, but about discovering the common ground among them.

questions_es.question_es: What does the passage suggest instéd of shedding all masks?

c1-essay_2.body_es: The desire to be recognized by someone is not something to be ashamed of; it is a natural human need. This need can also become a driving force that leads us in a better direction. But the story changes when gaining recognition becomes the sole purpose of life. Those who rely too heavily on others' evaluations gradually lose the ability to judge for themselves what they actually want. An even bigger problem is that the standard for recognition usually lies in others' hands, not one's own. So no matter how hard one tries, moments of failing to receive satisfying recognition can keep repeating. A healthy attitude is not to abandon recognition entirely but to adjust its wocho. It is far more stable to first establish an internal standard for recognizing yourself, and to accept external recognition as a bonus. Doing so allows us to live together within relationships without being swayed by others' reactions.

questions_es.question_es: What do people lose by relying too heavily on others' evaluations?
options: The ability to judge what they want

questions_es.question_es: What does the writer suggest treating external recognition as?

c1-essay_3.body_es: Many people treat self-esteem and self-efficacy as the same thing, but they are subtly different concepts. Self-esteem is valuing yourself as you are, while self-efficacy is the belief that you can accomplish a specific task. Someuno with low self-esteem can still have high self-efficacy in a particular field, and the reverse is just as possible. This distinction matters because we often try to fill our self-esteem with achievements. Getting a good score on a test or succeeding in a project will certainly raise self-efficacy. But that achievement does not automatically translate into respecting yourself. In fact, if you rely solely on achievements to support your self-esteem, you can easily fall into the illusion that your whole self collapses the moment you fail. That's why experts advise cultivating self-respect separately, regardless of achievement. Skill can be honed, but respect for oneself should be preserved regardless of outcome.

questions_es.question_es: ¿qué es self-efficacy defined as?

c1-essay_4.title_es: The wocho of a perfect image
c1-essay_4.body_es: The desire to maintain a flawless image looks at first like a sign of diligence, but underneath lies considerable anxiety. That anxiety is the fear that the moment a single mistake is revealed, the entire image built up will collapse. Such people spend a great deal of energy showing a life with no visible cracks. But no matter how hard they try, a perfect image only keeps widening the gap with the real self. As that gap grows, people become more guarded about being caught as their real selves, which actually makes relationships shallower. Paradoxically, the people others open their hearts to most are not the perfect unos, but those who can admit their own shortcomings. Showing a gap is not revealing a weakness but giving the other person room to approach. Therefore, practicing comfortable acceptance of oneself as one is builds far greater trust than effort spent protecting a perfect image.

options: The gap with the real self

c1-essay_5.body_es: Seeing yourself objectively is not as easy as it sounds. Everyone tends to interpret things about themselves in a favorable direction. A typical example is crojoiting good outcomes to one's own effort while blaming bad outcomes on circumstance or luck. This bias helps protect self-esteem, but it can also become an obstacle to growth. Failing to accurately see one's own shortcomings increases the likelihood of repeating the same mistakes. That's why feedback from trustworthy others becomes a valuable resource for self-objectification. That doesn't mean accepting all feedback at face value, however. It's important to pick out the patterns that repeatedly appear across several people's opinions. A trait that consistently shows up across various contexts is a far more reliable clue than one or two people's momentary evaluation. In the end, self-objectification is not self-deprecation but a tool for accurately grasping who you are in order to move in a better direction.

questions_es.question_es: What bias does the passage describe regarding good and bad outcomes?
options: Crojoiting good outcomes to effort, blaming bad ones on luck

questions_es.question_es: ¿qué tipo de feedback is most reliable, per the passage?
options: Patterns consisdiezt across several people and contexts

c1-essay_6.body_es: Many people want to find meaning in their work, but often can't clearly explain what that meaning actually is. It's easy to assume meaning only comes from a grand mission or a large impact on society. But actual research shows meaning more often comes not from the scale of the work but from who and how it connects to. For example, studies show that when a hospital janitor perceives their job not as mere cleaning but as part of the process helping patients recover, they feel far greater satisfaction in the same work. This shows that the perspective one holds, more than the nature of the work itself, determines its meaning. Of course, changing perspective alone doesn't solve every problem with working conditions. Unfair treatment or excessive workload are separate issues that must be addressed on their own. Still, the habit of concretely imagining who one's work affects and how becomes a practical way to find meaning even within the same job.

options: Salary is the only source of meaning

questions_es.question_es: What does the passage say changing perspective aluno cannot solve?

c1-essay_7.body_es: Burnout seems to arrive suddenly one day, but it's actually the result of small signals accumulating over a long time while being ignorojo. In its early stage, it's easy to mistake for simple fatigue, so many people brush it off. But over time, this fatigue spreads into a cynical attitude toward work or a sense of helplessness. A typical sign is feeling nothing at all even in tasks one used to be passionate about. The problem is that once it reaches this stage, simple rest alone doesn't make recovery easy. Burnout is not personal weakness but a phenomenon that arises from the interplay of an unsustainable work structure and one's own coping style. That's why experts stress that preventing burnout requires noticing the signals at a much earlier stage, before extreme exhaustion sets in. It's important not to ignore the moment when minor irritation increases or interest in work gradually fades. In the end, the best way to prevent burnout is to admit to yourself that you are already becoming exhausted, before you are completely worn out.

questions_es.question_es: ¿qué es burnout described as, rather than personal weakness?
options: An interplay of unsustainable structure and coping style

options: noticing signals at an early stage

c1-essay_8.body_es: Everyone has experienced being so absorbed in something that time seemed to disappear. Psychologists call this state of flow, and have long studied the conditions for it. Interestingly, flow doesn't happen with just any task. It arrives only when the difficulty of the task and one's skill level are appropriately balanced. Tasks that are too easy breed boredom, and tasks that are too hard breed anxiety, both of which block flow. That's why people who often experience flow have the ability to adjust the difficulty of a task themselves to match their skill. Another important condition is clear goals and immediate feedback. When we clearly know what to do right now and can immediately cuenta the result, we can stay fully in the moment without wandering thoughts. In the end, flow is not a special talent but something that begins with consciously arranging a few conditions: task, skill, goals, and feedback.

c1-essay_9.title_es: Career as a curve, not a ladder
c1-essay_9.body_es: We often imagine a career as a ladder we climb one rung at a time. But looking at many people's actual careers, they resemble a winding curve more than a ladder. There are periods of rapid growth, and periods of stagnation or even what feels like stepping backward. The problem is that people accustomed to the ladder model tend to interpret such stagnation and retreat as failure. As a result, they don't even allow themselves time to pause and cuenta their direction. But from the perspective of a curve, a period of stagnation can be a natural stretch preparing for the next leap, not a failure. Indeed, looking at many success stories, it's not uncommon for periods that seemed stagnant on the surface — learning a new skill, exploring a different field — to have driven the growth that followed. Therefore, when evaluating a career, an attitude that looks at the long-term trajectory rather than one's current position is necessary. Viewing your career as a curve rather than a ladder gives you room not to push yourself even during a stagnant moment.

c1-essay_10.body_es: Retirement is seen as a time of freedom from long labor, but for many it's also a time that brings an unexpected sense of loss. Once the seat one commuted to every day disappears, the daily rhythm that filled one's time disappears with it. A more fundamental problem is that the self, long explained by a title or role, is suddenly left with no modifier at all. This sense of loss is not a matter of laziness or weakness but a natural response to losing one major axis of identity. That's why it's important for those approaching retirement to prepare other ways of defining themselves in advance. Taking on new learning or reconnecting with long-neglected relationships are also good approaches. Interestingly, what people who remain actively engaged after retirement commonly emphasize is small goals. Modest routines one can practice daily, rather than grand plans, restore rhythm to post-retirement life. In the end, retirement may not be an ending but another starting point for rojoefining oneself.

options: A natural response to losing an axis of identity

c1-essay_11.body_es: Work that repeats in the same sequence every day is easily seen as meaningless. It seems to leave no room for creativity and to bring no change. But several studies interviewing people who have long done repetitive labor show an unexpected result. Quite a few of them found their own rhythm and the joy of mastery within the repetition. Subtle changes — a fingertip sense growing more refined, a motion slightly smoother than ayer — gave them ample satisfaction. This shows that meaning doesn't necessarily come only from grand change or novelty. However, discovering such meaning is premised on at least a minimal degree of autonomy being guaranteed. When one can adjust the order or method of work even slightly on one's own, repetition is experienced not as oppression but as a process of mastery. In the end, whether repetitive work is meaningless depends not on the form of labor but on whether one can find autonomy and mastery within it.

Their own rhythm and joy of mastery

c1-essay_12.body_es: The advice to turn what you love into your job has long been repeated like a formula for success. This advice sounds appealing at first, but a trap lurks beneath it that gets overlooked. Discourse that emphasizes passion tends to make demands for fair working conditions or pay secondary. It easily leads to the logic that, since you love it, you should endure the hardship. In fact, this logic is often mobilized to justify low pay and overwork even in fields socially recognized as valuable, like art or caregiving. Moreover, the belief that passion aluno leads to success ends up placing the full responsibility for failure on the individual. Structural problems and elements of luck get erased, leaving only self-blame for lacking passion. That doesn't mean love or interest in one's work doesn't matter. But we need to look a bit more critically at whether the word 'passion' is being used as a shield to hide unfair treatment.

c1-essay_13.body_es: Refusing a request is easily seen as damaging a relationship, but it's actually an essential skill for maintaining a healthy one. Many people, fearing that the other person will be hurt or the relationship will grow distant, force themselves to accept requests they don't want to take on. But when this pattern repeats, one ends up piling up burdens too heavy to bear. Suppressed burden inevitably surfaces in some form, usually as visible irritation or unconscious distancing. Interestingly, an appropriate refusal actually raises trust in a relationship. It's hard to tell whether the agreement of someone who always says yes is sincere or merely a ritual, whereas the agreement of someone who can say no becomes, in itself, a trustworthy signal. Of course, how one refuses matters too. Respecting the other person's request while clearly conveying one's own limits is the core of refusing without damaging the relationship. In the end, learning to refuse well is not a selpescado attitude but the wisdom of sustaining a relationship longer.

c1-essay_14.body_es: When we drift apart from an old friend, we often consider that relationship a failure. But the idea that every relationship must last a lifetime may oversimplify the nature of relationships. People keep changing over time, and the speed and direction of that change differ from friend to friend. Even a bond that once sharojo the same worries will naturally find fewer shared topics as each person's life phase diverges. Defining this drifting apart as failure leaves only guilt or a sense of loss behind. But accepting that the relationship already played its full role for what each needed at the time makes the same situation feel much calmer. Interestingly, this calm acceptance actually makes us value the relationships that remain even more. Rather than forcing yourself to cling to every bond, accepting that each has its own shelf life ultimately creates a healthier network of relationships.

c1-essay_15.body_es: The desire to avoid conflict is natural, since facing uncomfortable emotions is a burden for anyone. But if conflict is constantly avoided, a relationship only appears calm on the surface while unresolved problems quietly pile up underneath. In order to preserve surface-level peace, genuinely important disagreements remain sealed away. The problem is that such accumulated conflict eventually leads to a far bigger explosion at an unexpected moment. When a trivial trigger causes long-suppressed emotions to burst out all at once, the actual substance of the conflict gets blurred, leaving only an emotional fight. By contrast, relationships that handle conflict as it arises tend to grow sturdier instéd. That's because the very experience of a relationship surviving conflict becomes an asset that builds trust. Therefore, the common belief that avoiding conflict is the way to preserve a relationship deserves reconsideration.

c1-essay_16.body_es: Family is seen as the closest presence in the world, yet at the same time it's a relationship where people often understand each other the least. The fact of having spent a long time together creates the illusion of fully knowing one another. This illusion can also cause people to neglect conversation. What one would carefully explain to a friend gets skipped with family, assuming they'll understand without being told. But family members, too, are individuals who keep changing over time. The assumption that who they were ayer is exactly who they are today is often wrong. So, if anything, family calls for treating each other like strangers — asking and confirming anew. Rather than assuming based on familiarity, the effort to get to know who the other person is now keeps the relationship fresh. In the end, the closeness of family is not something maintained automatically; it's a relationship that deepens by acknowledging unfamiliarity.

c1-essay_17.body_es: Trust builds up little by little over a long time, but often collapses in an instant. Interestingly, what usually breaks trust is not a single major betrayal but the repetition of small inconsistencies. When minor promises are broken repeatedly, each one might be resolved with an apology, but once they accumulate, the very predictability of the other person is shaken. People don't expect the other person to be perfect; they want the other's words and actions to be consistent. That's why the attitude after a mistake affects trust more than the mistake itself. Someone who acknowledges a mistake and shows concrete improvement can actually restore trust, while someone who keeps making excuses loses trust completely even over a small error. Restoring trust once it's broken takes several times more time and effort than building it did. Therefore, the surest way to protect trust in a relationship is not keeping big promises but the stédiness of not breaking small ones.

c1-essay_18.body_es: It's common to feel deep loneliness even while surrounded by people. That's because loneliness arrives more powerfully from a lack of emotional connection than from physical solitude. Even if people are conversing in the same space, if that conversation stays at the level of surface pleasantries, each person remains on their own isla. Interestingly, this loneliness stems not from the quantity of relationships but from their quality. No matter how many acquaintances one has, loneliness won't disappear if there's no one to share one's real thoughts and feelings with. Conversely, even a single deep connection can resolve much of this loneliness. So rather than focusing solely on widening one's circle, it's often more effective to check the depth of the relationships one already has. In the end, the reason we feel lonely even together is not a lack of people nearby, but a lack of moments to share one's real self.

questions_es.question_es: What does lunoliness stem from, per the passage?

c1-essay_19.body_es: The number of decisions we have to make in a day is far greater than we think. From what to wear in the mañana to what to eat for lunch to which approach to take at work, big and small decisions follow one another endlessly. The problem is that these decisions gradually deplete mental resources. The phenomenon in which the very ability to make decisions grows exhausted as the day goes on is called decision fatigue. Interestingly, as decision fatigue accumulates, people tend to make increasingly impulsive choices, or conversely, avoid making any decision at all. This is not a lack of willpower but the result of actually depleted resources. That's why it's advantageous to make important decisions early in the day, when mental resources are still plentiful. Also, presetting minor decisions as habits or rules can save the resources needed for more important decisions. In the end, the ability to make good decisions is less a matter of innate willpower than a matter of how one allocates finite mental resources.

c1-essay_20.body_es: Boredom is usually seen as an uncomfortable feeling to be avoided. As long as a smartphone is in hand, we tend to reach for the screen the instant even a brief moment of boredom sets in. But several recent studies show that boredom is closely linked to creativity. During a period with no particular stimulation, the brain actually begins to freely wander among thoughts that don't normally connect. Indeed, there are many reports of creative ideas arising during moments when one isn't particularly focused — while washing dishes or taking a walk, for instance. The problem is that we can't tolerate such boring moments and fill the gap with immediate stimulation instéd. As a result, the very opportunity for the brain to organize its own thoughts and form new connections is disappearing. So deliberately securing time without stimulation can actually help productivity. In the end, boredom is not a problem to be eliminated but a blank space that should be preserved for creative thinking.

c1-essay_21.body_es: Procrastination is often seen as a problem of laziness, but in reality a far more complex emotional mechanism is at work. In many cases, procrastination comes not from a lack of ability but from a fear of failure. If you don't start, at least no definite evidence of failure remains. This psychology operates more strongly especially when expectations for the outcome are high, or when the pressure to do it perfectly is great. Interestingly, the mind is never at ease even while procrastinating. Guilt and anxiety about postponing what needs to be done constantly linger in the background, so procrastination is not rest but another form of drain. That's why overcoming procrastination is more effectively achieved not by pushing willpower but by breaking a task into much smaller units. Lowering the starting threshold to a small action doable within cinco minutes, instead of a grand goal, reduces the pressure to be perfect and makes it far easier to actually move. In the end, the power to beat procrastination comes not from steeling one's resolve but from lowering the threshold of starting.

c1-essay_22.body_es: The red numbers that pop up on our phone screens hijack our attention dozens of times a day. What was originally designed for convenience has quietly become a signal that dictates the rhythm of our lives. People habitually cuenta their screens even when no notification has sounded, and even that brief check disrupts full concentration. The problem is not any single notification but the chronic distraction that accumulates from them. We are slowly being trained to care more about the next piece of news than about the task at hand. Interestingly, simply turning off notifications does not easily erase this habit. Because the brain has already learned a circuit that expects stimulation, fingers move on their own even in front of a silent screen. That is why some experts say that conscious training to reclaim attention matters more than technical fixes for managing notifications. In the end, the way out of the tyranny of notifications lies not in blaming the device but in choosing again what we respond to. Only when such small choices accumulate does control over the day return to us.

c1-essay_23.body_es: When you visit a portal site, headlines full of sensational phrases compete for your attention. Words like 'shocking,' 'stunning,' and 'twist' are now designed to trigger emotion before conveying any actual content. Under a structure where a single reader click translates directly into revenue, media outlets are pushed into a race to intensify sensationalism. As a result, when readers actually open the article, the event is often far less dramatic than the headline implied. Repeated experiences like this gradually erode readers' trust in headlines themselves, yet their hands still click on them again. This is because a stimulating phrase triggers a reaction before rational judgment can intervene. A more serious problem is that this headline competition has reshaped how news itself is produced, prioritizing emotional intensity over factual accuracy. In the end, what readers gain is not information but momentary stimulation, and once that stimulation fades, only an emptiness remains where they cannot even recall what they read. To reverse this trend, readers themselves must cultivate the habit of judging the crojoibility of the body text rather than the headline.

c1-essay_24.body_es: We often mistake opinions that appear frequently online for public opinion. But it is easy to forget that only a tiny fraction of all users actually speak up. When a small group of vocal commenters posts repeatedly, algorithms interpret that activity as popularity and expose it to even more people. The result is an illusion in which an opinion far removed from the silent majority appears to represent everyone's voice. This mirage grows thicker especially around controversial topics. People with stronger emotions have greater motivation to post their opinions multiple times. Quiet observers grow intimidated by this intense atmosphere and withdraw further into silence, which makes the minority's voice ring relatively louder. In the end, the public opinion we see on screen is not a miniature of actual public sentiment but a biased sample of ¿quién es willing to speak. If we judge the world by online reactions alone without recognizing this, we end up chasing the shadow of a majority that does not truly exist.

They interpret frequent posting as popularity

c1-essay_25.body_es: mils of articles and posts pass under our fingertips every day. In the era of information scarcity, knowing was itself power, but now the more important skill is deciding what to filter out. Amid the flood of information, people have grown used to judging by headlines and summaries rather than reading deeply. This habit gives the illusion of having encountered a lot of information in a short time, but in reality nothing is fully digested before moving on to the next item. Psychologists describe this as a phenomenon in which the volume of information and the depth of understanding move in inverse proportion. Especially when contradictory information floods in at once, people tend to take the shortcut of choosing what they already believed rather than suspending judgment. As a result, a paradox emerges in which thinking becomes simpler even as information grows more abundant. In this environment, what may truly be needed is not more information but the habit of slowly chewing over less of it. In the end, the wisdom of living in an age of information overload lies not in deciding what to see more of, but in deciding what not to see.

More information leads to simpler thinking

c1-essay_26.body_es: The screens we access every day each wear a different face. The reason different people get different results even for the same search term is that algorithms learn individual tastes and behaviors and edit the world accordingly before showing it to us. This editing is meant for convenience, but it also quietly narrows the range of the world we see. The problem is that this editing is invisible. We feel as though we are freely exploring information on our own, but in reality we are only choosing among options that have already been filtered. As a result, people from different backgrounds form their thoughts within entirely different information environments even when discussing the same event. When this repeats, it becomes increasingly difficult to hold conversations on a shared factual foundation. This is because people mistakenly believe they are discussing the same world even as they are actually looking at different ones. To narrow this gap, we need the effort to consciously seek out the areas algorithms do not show us. The habit of stepping outside the edited world is the minimal way to preserve a balanced perspective hoy.

c1-essay_27.title_es: The Arithmetic of the Atdieztion Economy
c1-essay_27.body_es: It is no longer surprising to hear that the most valuable resource today is not money but people's attention. Countless free services actually operate by taking our time and gaze as payment. Because the time users spend on a screen directly converts into advertising revenue, companies meticulously refine designs meant to hold us as long as possible. Infinite scrolling and features that auto-play the next video are not accidents but the products of careful calculation. Within this structure, we believe we are choosing to watch the screen ourselves, but in many cases we are merely reacting to engineered stimuli. The problem is that this arithmetic is too sophisticated for individual willpower alone to counter. It is not easy for an individual to consciously resist, every single time, a design built by ciens of experts using psychology and data. That is why, recently, voices calling for accountability in service design itself, rather than emphasizing individual restraint, have grown louder. In the end, understanding the arithmetic of the attention economy is not merely a matter of self-management but also a question of who is taking the value of our time.

options: Converting user atdieztion time into advertising revenue

From individual restraint to service design accountability

c1-essay_28.body_es: Recommendations tailorojo to our interests feel very convenient at first. Since content we are likely to enjoy comes to us automatically, there is no need to make an effort to explore. But this convenience gradually results in trapping us inside a thin membrane. Topics outside our interest and opposing opinions gradually vanish from our screens, and we end up hearing, again and again, only voices that think similarly to us. Staying in such an environment for a long time makes it easy to fall into the illusion that one's own view represents the majority. In reality, we are only looking at a narrow world edited in a particular direction. An even bigger problem is that this membrane is invisible. Transparent like a glass wall, it lets us feel comfortable without even recognizing that we are enclosed. Escaping this comfort requires deliberately seeking out unfamiliar perspectives and uncomfortable opinions. In the end, the first step out of the filter bubble must begin not with the algorithm but with our own curiosity.

options: Believing uno's view represents the majority

c1-essay_29.body_es: Memes made of a single short image and a few phrases are often dismissed as light jokes. But looked at closely, few formats compress the emotional mood of an era as effectively as memes do. What a long editorial cannot explain — a generation's fatigue or its cynicism toward society — a meme conveys in mere seconds. This stems from the paradox that a comical format actually makes a heavy truth easier to accept. A story that would provoke backlash if stated bluntly can be heard without defensiveness when pairojo with humor. Of course, this format also carries the risk of oversimplifying complex contexts. When subtle differences disappear and everything is compressed into a single image, the important details of a debate can easily be obscured. Even so, the fact that memes spread quickly and stay in circulation for a long time is also evidence that they resonate with many people. In the end, rather than viewing memes as a passing fad, we need to read the collective emotion embedded within them. Not missing the heavy truth hidden behind the light laughter — that is how to properly read a meme.

options: Memes require no context to understand
Comical format makes heavy truths easier to accept

They cost too much to produce

c1-essay_30.body_es: Short videos that jump to the next scene within seconds now dominate many people's leisure time. This format is so powerful precisely because it leaves no room for boredom. The moment interest dips even slightly, a single finger swipe moves to the next video, so the brain continuously receives only peak-level stimulation. The problem is that a brain accustomed to such stimulation gradually becomes unable to tolerate slower-paced content. A growing number of people confess that even a few-minute documentary feels boring, and reading a single page of a book feels far more difficult than it used to. This is not simply a shift in taste but a sign that the very capaciudad to sustain attention is being reshaped. Of course, not all short videos can be declared harmful; many serve as a useful format for compressing information into a short span. But the problem is not the format itself, but the way it becomes a habit that crowds out other forms of immersion. In the end, resisting the temptation of short-form video requires consciously protecting time set aside for longer-breathing content.

options: They become unable to tolerate slower-paced condiezt
They lose interest in all video condiezt
They become better at reading books

options: The low quality of short-form condiezt
The habit crowding out other forms of immersion
The cost of producing short videos
The lack of regulation on video platforms

c1-essay_31.body_es: In online spaces, we encounter countless writings by other people every day, yet we rarely imagine what face they wore while writing them. Having grown used to judging based on a few lines of text, we easily forget that there is a person with feelings on the other side of the screen. This forgetting is especially pronounced around controversial topics. When rebutting someone's opinion, we often hurl sharp words directly at the person themselves — words we would likely never say if that person were standing in front of us. Psychologists explain this as an illusion of psychological distance created by physical distance. Because the screen, as a medium, reduces another person's presence to abstract text, the circuitry of empathy operates less than it normally would. The problem is that this attitude does not stay confined online but gradually seeps into how we converse in real life as well. To prevent this, some people recommend the habit of imagining that the other person is actually standing in front of you before writing. It may seem trivial, but simply recalling that there is a life of equal wocho to one's own beyond the screen can change the temperature of one's words.

options: As a result of gobierno policy
As an illusion of psychological distance from physical distance
As a natural human instinct with no cause

options: Imagining the other person is physically present before writing

c1-essay_32.body_es: A single piece of paperwork encounterojo at an administrative window compresses a person's story into numbers and categories. The moment major life events — birth, marriage, moving, employment — are filled into standardized boxes, the complex context of each individual disappears into a uniform format. This compression is an unavoidable choice for administrative efficiency, but it is also a mirror revealing how the system views people. This is because the items a form requires become the very standard by which that society judges individuals. For instance, if a form proving family relationships presumes only a traditional family structure, people who fall outside that form experience exclusion from the very moment they try to fill it in. Such exclusion may seem trivial, but when repeated, it can lead to fundamental distrust of institutions. Interestingly, even a small change to a form's structure can suddenly make visible the people it previously failed to capture. In the end, paperwork is not merely an administrative tool but a miniature of society showing whom it assumes as the default and whom it treats as the exception. Redesigning paperwork is therefore not a trivial administrative task but a way of re-questioning how a society sees itself.

questions_es.question_es: What does the essay say paperwork requirements reveal?
options: The number of civil servants employed
How a society judges and categorizes individuals

questions_es.question_es: What effect can a small change to a form's structure have?
options: It can make previously invisible people visible

c1-essay_33.body_es: An exam appears to be forgotten once it ends, but in reality it leaves traces in our thinking for a long time. Solving problems with predetermined correct answers repeatedly instills, almost unconsciously, a belief that every question in the world has one certain answer. This belief may have been an efficient learning strategy during escuela years, but it becomes an obstacle when facing real-world problems that lack a clear answer. Many people, even after entering society, still wait for someone to tell them the correct answer and struggle to judge and decide for themselves. Moreover, because exams prioritize the ability to produce accurate answers quickly, the mindset of slowly pondering and exploring multiple possibilities is relatively undertrained. This can emerge as an unexpected weakness in situations that demand creativity or flexible problem-solving. Of course, the institution of examinations itself cannot be dismissed, since it remains necessary as a minimal device for fairly gauging ability. Still, one must not forget to recognize the habits exams leave behind and separately cultivate the strength to think independently even when facing questions without a clear answer.

options: That every question has uno certain answer

questions_es.question_es: What weakness can this belief create later in life?
options: Difficulty judging and deciding independently on unclear problems

c1-essay_34.body_es: The word bureaucracy usually carries a negative impression, conjuring slow processing, formalistic procedure, and people passing responsibility onto uno another. But looking back at the original purpose for which bureaucracy was devised tells a somewhat different story. Applying the same procedure to everyone according to fixed regulations was originally designed to prevent the unfairness that arbitrary individual judgment could cause. The problem arises when this principle is applied too rigidly. An attitude that merely repeats regulations without exercising flexibility even in exceptional situations betrays the very purpose bureaucracy was meant to serve. Interestingly, even people who criticize bureaucracy demand exception-free application of rules precisely in situations where they themselves stand to be disadvantaged. This well illustrates the dual nature of bureaucracy. The two faces — a shield protecting fairness and a heartless wall — actually stem from a single principle. In the end, the way to improve bureaucracy lies not in eliminating it but in carefully carving out room within the system for principle and flexibility to coexist.

questions_es.question_es: What was bureaucracy originally designed to prevent, per the essay?

options: They demand exception-free rules when it benefits them
They prefer no rules at all

c1-essay_35.body_es: Everyone has experienced the moment their fingers reach for a screen automatically even when there is nothing in particular to cuenta. This behavior is less a conscious decision than a reflex etched into the body. Repeated actions carve out automated pathways in the brain that execute with less and less effort, and the habit of checking a smartphone is no exception to this principle. The problem is that this habit forms far faster than it can be undone. Just a few days of repetition is enough to entrench an automated behavior, but reversing it requires far longer and more conscious effort. Interestingly, people move their hands without even noticing in the moment, even while being aware of the habit in general. This is because a defining feature of automated behavior is that it occurs without conscious intervention. Attempts to break free of such habits usually rely on willpower, but willpower has the limitation of being an easily depleted resource. That is why recent research increasingly finds it more effective to redesign the environment so the device is out of reach from the start — for instance, physically leaving it in another room — rather than demanding willpower. In the end, changing habits at our fingertips is less a matter of steeling one's mind than of redesigning the environment.

options: It is an easily depleted resource

options: Punishing oneself for cuentaing the phone
rojoesigning the environment so the device is out of reach

c1-essay_36.body_es: A day when a phone's battery dies completely brings an unexpected experience. The first few hours are dominated by anxiety and restlessness — thoughts about missing an important call, or whether someone is trying to reach you, circle the mind. But as time passes, this anxiety gradually shifts into a different sensation. Moments that would normally be spent staring at a screen begin to come into sharp focus. Things that were always there but never registered — the scenery outside a window, the expressions of passersby — reveal their presence anew. This experience paradoxically makes us realize how often we had drifted away from the present moment into somewhere else inside a screen. Interestingly, this realization fades quickly the moment the battery is recharged. As soon as the connection is restored, we habitually cuenta the screen again and forget the quiet we had just experienced. This shows that the insight disconnection provides does not persist on its own and disappears quickly unless consciously held onto. In the end, the real lesson a day without battery leaves behind is that we sometimes need to deliberately set aside time to disconnect ourselves.

options: It sharpens, noticing previously unnoticed details

options: It fades quickly unless consciously held onto

c1-essay_37.body_es: Confessions of feeling isolated despite a friend list of ciens and a constant stream of messages are no longer unusual. This phenomenon looks contradictory at first glance, but on closer look it has its own logic. An increase in the quantity of connection does not necessarily mean an increase in its quality as well. Communication made up of short messages and light reactions is effective at maintaining superficial contact but rarely develops into a relationship of deep understanding and shared vulnerability. In fact, the more such shallow connections increase, the easier it is for people to fall into the illusion that they are sufficiently socially connected, and that illusion makes them neglect the effort to newly build deeper relationships. Interestingly, people who feel connected loneliness tend to increase their online activity even more. They try to fill an unfulfilled emptiness with more contact, but as long as the quality of that contact does not change, the emptiness does not disappear. This is similar to trying to quench thirst with salt water. In the end, the way out of connected loneliness lies not in increasing the quantity of contact but in the deliberate effort to deepen even a small number of relationships.

c1-essay_38.body_es: Understanding aging only as a list of losses is far too narrow a view. Of course it is hard to deny that stamina and speed are not what they were. Yet there are areas where the accuracy of judgment actually becomes more refined with experience. If youth is a time of possibility, the years after midlife are closer to a time of choice. That is because knowing what not to do is also a kind of ability. The problem is that society treats aging as a risk to be managed. Within such a view, old age is merely an object of preparation and is not respected as a phase of life. We should ask not about a society that lives long but uno that lives meaningfully until late.

c1-story_0.title_es: The umbrella at the bus stop
c1-story_0.body_es: By the time she realized the last bus had already gone, she was half soaked. A stranger stood under the shelter roof, and for a long while the two of them treated each other as if invisible. When the rain thickened, the man silently tilted his umbrella halfway toward her, and instead of thanking him, she simply stared at the streetlamp. In the quince or so minutes before a taxi came, they exchanged only a few words about the weather and the last bus, never asking each other's names. c1-story_1.title_es: The hands that fold paper cranes
c1-story_1.body_es: Every evening after dinner, the grandfather would take out a sheet of colored paper and fold a crane. No matter how many times his granddaughter asked, he never once explained why he did it or who it was for. His drawer held hundreds of cranes, neatly sorted by color, and a few among them were noticeably worn and faded. After he passed away, while sorting through his belongings, his granddaughter found an old letter at the bottom of the drawer. It was addressed to a younger brother he had been separated from during the war, a letter he had never managed to send, and it carried a childhood belief that folding a mil cranes would bring them back together. c1-story_2.body_es: The only thing among his father's belongings that wasn't worth any money was that wristwatch. It was an old wind-up model, its glass marked with a thin crack. The siblings divided the house and bank accounts evenly, but when it came to the watch, each seemed to defer to the others, and no one offered to take it first. As the youngest, he one day absentmindedly took the watch from a drawer and wound it, and the sound of the second hand starting to move again strangely put his mind at ease. Only later did he learn from his mother that his father had bought it with his very first paycuenta and had worn it his whole life, fixing it whenever it broke. c1-story_3.body_es: Under the fluorescent lights of the hospital waiting room, the two of them had been sitting side by side for two hours. One was waiting for test results, the other for news of a husband about to go into surgery. At first neither so much as glanced at the other, but each time an announcement came over the speakers, the small flinch of raising their heads had, without either noticing, come to look the same. In the end it was the woman, getting coffee from the vending machine, who spoke first, and the man took the paper cup with a brief thanks. Before they had exchanged more than a few words that could hardly be called a conversation, the woman's name was called, and before standing she left him with the words that it would turn out fine. He declined at first, but couldn't refuse when the man held it out a second time, and took it. As he peeled it, the old man, gazing at the snow outside the window, began telling him how he had first met his wife during a snowstorm just like this one, years ago. It was nothing extraordinary, but in the old man's profile reflected in the dark glass, an expression flickered as though that time were still alive somewhere inside him. When the train started moving again, the old man simply closed his eyes without finishing the story, and he did not press him for the rest. When they parted ways at their destination, he realized only belatedly that he didn't even know the old man's name.

c1-story_5.body_es: Returning to his old neighborhood after veinte years, even the width of the alley felt unfamiliar. Where the stationery shop used to stand, a franchise convenience store now sat, and the persimmon tree he used to peer over the low wall to see had vanished without a trace. He found his eyes unconsciously tracing the pattern of the pavement he had walked every day as a child, but even that had been replaced with new tiles. The only thing that remained exactly as it was stood at the end of the alley: the gate, its paint redone but the position of the handle and the tilt of the frame unchanged. He stood before it a moment, wavering over whether to press the bell, then turned away without doing so. c1-story_6.body_es: Every mañana on the same bus, she found herself watching the man who always sat in the very back. At each stop where an elderly passenger got on, he would quietly rise from his seat, pretending to look out the window, and the seat would soon naturally belong to someone else. He never once said aloud that he was giving up his seat, and even when thanked, he only gave a small nod. One day she happened to walk in the same direction as him after getting off at his stop, but she didn't bother speaking to him. c1-story_7.body_es: She rememberojo that fight starting from the moment her husband raised his voice, while he remembered it starting from the moment she slammed the door. Years later, when the argument happened to come up again, they both fell briefly silent upon realizing how differently each of them had been holding onto the scene. She believed she had endured as much as she could before reacting; he believed she had trampled the very moment he was about to apologize first. There was no longer any way to confirm whose memory was closer to the truth. The one thing that matched exactly was that both of them had grown a little more careful with each other after that day. c1-story_8.body_es: On the day the laundromat he had run for thirty years finally closed, he took one last look around the empty shop before pulling down the shutter. Beside the sewing machine, clothes that customers had dropped off long ago and never come back for still hung on their hangers. When one of his regular customers, an elderly woman, heard the news and stopped by one last time to hand him a cup of café, he tried to say it was fine but found his throat too tight for any words. She offered no particular words of comfort, simply looked around the shop once and stood there quietly. She stayed standing outside until the shutter was fully down, and that alone told him thirty years hadn't been for nothing. Watching her walk away down the alley, he found himself unable to lock the shutter for a long while.

c1-story_9.body_es: Around the age of veinte, she once wrote a letter to a first love she had just broken up with. She wrote down everything she wanted to say, but the moment she went to write the address on the envelope, her hand stopped, and the letter ended up spending twenty years inside her desk drawer. Every so often, whenever she tidied the drawer, the letter was always still there, and each time, unable to either throw it away or send it, she simply closed the drawer again. Recently, while packing to move, she unfolded the letter and read it again, and now the sentences inside felt as though a stranger had written them. Instead of sending it, she quietly burned it, and watching the paper turn to ash, she felt, oddly, more relief than sorrow. Only then did she come to understand that some feelings can be complete even without ever being delivered.

c1-story_10.body_es: On his way home from work, when the sun hung low and red between the rooftops, he would deliberately take the narrow alley instead of the main street. At that hour, the alley, filled with the mixed smell of dinner cooking and the sound of televisions, had a way of loosening something tight in him. It wasn't the neighborhood he'd grown up in, but watching the lights spill through the windows somehow brought back the image of himself sitting at the dinner table long ago. Having gone through a string of small and large disappointments at work recently, he had come to see this short walk as the one time of day he could quietly comfort himself. Nothing in particular was ever resolved, but by the time he emerged from the alley onto the main street, the tension in his shoulders had eased somewhat. Today, too, he walked that alley in silence, and mañana he would likely choose the same road.

c1-story_11.body_es: Two months before his mother passed away, he happened to stop by his childhood home and had dinner alone with her. It wasn't a special meal, and the conversation was no different from usual, but that day she kept pushing side dishes toward his rice bowl. He ate without much thought and left in a hurry without even doing the dishes, having no idea it would be the last meal he'd ever share with her. Months after the funeral, eating alone one day, he suddenly began recalling, one by one, the small details of that noche. His mother's gestures, where the side dish bowls had sat, even the sunset fading outside the window — all of it grew belatedly vivid. c1-story_12.body_es: Every Sunday evening, she would call her aunt, who lived out of town, to check in. For years she had never once skipped that call, but one Sunday, after calling three times with no answer, she thought nothing of it. When the next day passed, and the day after that, still without a call back, an inexplicable unease began creeping in. Just as she was about to reach out to her aunt's daughter, the phone rang; the caller was an unfamiliar number, and the voice belonged to a nurse from the hospital her aunt had been attending. Listening to the calm explanation on the other end, she found herself, oddly, recalling the unanswered ringing tone from that past Sunday before any tears came. Only then, belatedly, did she realize that those three unanswered calls had already been telling her something.
