c1-story_13.body_es: When she heard that her grandson had graduated and received his first paycuenta, the grandmother offered the same kind of blessing she always had — that he should find stable work at a good company and settle down. Grateful as he was for the words, the grandson chose not to mention that he was, in fact, working on a temporary contract. She belonged to a generation that stayed at one company until retirement; he belonged to one for whom changing jobs every few years was simply normal. The conversation flowed smoothly even without either of them truly understanding the other, and each time she brought up stability, he simply smiled and nodded. Near the end of the meal, she quietly pressed an envelope of money into his hand, and after declining once, he finally took it. Two people who had lived through different eras shared their hearts that way, over a single meal, in place of the word understanding.

questions_es.question_es: ¿qué hizo grandson not tell his grandmother?
options: That he had failed his exams
That he was working on a temporary contract
That he had quit his job

questions_es.question_es: ¿cómo passage describe the gap between the two generations?
options: It remained unspoken but the meal still connected them
It was fully resolved by the end

c1-story_14.body_es: He happened to learn that his coworker had been carrying a resignation letter in his bag for three months already. The corner of an envelope glimpsed during a meeting, the habit of cuentaing real estate apps every lunch hour, the noticeably quieter expression — all of it connected, belatedly, into one picture. The coworker never mentioned it to anyone, and he, for his part, never let on that he knew. But at a company dinner, when the coworker muttered, almost in passing, that he wasn't sure it was right to leave a stable position now, he could guess it was about the resignation letter. A few weeks later, the coworker's desk was still exactly the same, and the envelope was no longer visible. He never learned how that hesitation ended; he simply remained someone who had quietly witnessed another person lingering long at a fork in the road of his life.

questions_es.question_es: How did the narrator learn about the coworker's resignation letter?
options: He pieced it together from small observed details
He read it on the coworker's desk

questions_es.question_es: ¿qué es the state of things at the end of the passage?
options: The outcome remains unknown to the narrator
The narrator confronted the coworker directly

c1-story_15.body_es: The old man who had run the barbershop, its sign long since peeling, for nearly fifty years, had grown too weak-sighted even to handle the scissors well anymore. Once word spread through the neighborhood that this was the last day of business, old regulars who had rarely come by in recent years began showing up again, one after another. None of them said anything in particular; they simply sat in the chair as they always had, opening a newspaper or closing their eyes and leaving themselves to his hands. The old man, too, cut hair with his usual gruffness and handed back the change without saying a word about it being the last day. Just before closing, when the oldest regular left twice the usual price on the counter, the old man paused for a moment, at last, and looked out the window. The next mañana, the shutter never went back up.

questions_es.question_es: What happened once word spread that it was the barbertienda's last day?
options: Old regulars who rarely visited began coming back

questions_es.question_es: ¿qué hizo oldest regular do before leaving?
options: He asked the barber to reconsider
He left double the usual payment
He gave the barber a gift

c1-story_16.title_es: The photograph inside a used book
c1-story_16.body_es: Buying an old poetry collection at a used bookstore, he came home and, flipping through the pages, found an aged black-and-white photograph. In it, two escuelagirls in uniform were smiling, and on the back was written only a name and a date, nothing more. Not knowing what to do with it, he left the photograph on his desk for several days. There was no way to find the people in the picture, nor any clear reason he needed to, yet he felt he couldn't simply throw those faces away. In the end, he slipped the photograph back between the pages of the book and carefully placed it on his shelf, for whoever might open the book next. Perhaps, he thought, some connections are passed on this way, to the next person, without either of them ever knowing the other's name.

questions_es.question_es: ¿qué hizo man find inside the used poetry book?
options: An old photograph of two escuelagirls

questions_es.question_es: ¿qué hizo man ultimately decide to do with it?
options: Try to track down the people in it
Put it back in the book for a future reader

c1-story_17.body_es: Since retiring, he had gone out to the riverbank with his fishing rod almost every dawn, while the darkness had not yet fully lifted. Whether he caught anything or not seemed to matter little to him, and there were many mañanas when he simply sat for hours with his eyes on the water. In his younger years he had been known for a restlessness that could hardly sit still, yet now he seemed like a man for whom the mere sound of the flowing river was enough. Few people knew that he had begun keeping this hour after his wife passed away. When a passerby from the neighborhood occasionally greeted him, he answered briefly and turned his gaze back to the water. Only once the sun had fully risen did he fold up his rod and slowly rise to his feet.

questions_es.question_es: ¿qué es notably different about the man compared to his younger self?
options: He is now much more talkative
He used to be restless, but now finds the río's sound enough
He never used to like nature
He now avoids the outdoors entirely

questions_es.question_es: What does the passage suggest is behind his new habit?
options: A doctor recommended pescadoing for his health
It began after his wife's death, though few know this
He is trying to earn dinero from fishing
He is preparing to write a book about it

c1-story_18.title_es: The day we divided our parents' belongings
c1-story_18.body_es: After both their parents had passed away, the tres siblings gathered to clear out the old family house. There wasn't much of value; mostly worn dishes, old clothes, and furniture worn smooth by years of handling. And yet, whenever their wishes for the same item overlapped, an unexpected tension ran between them. In the end, the second sibling and the youngest quietly clashed over their mother's old sewing machine, and watching the scene, the eldest daughter could understand that what each of them truly wanted was not the object itself but something still carrying their mother's touch. In the end, she gave up her own claim on the sewing machine and instead took an old ladle tucked in the corner of the kitchen drawer. In that ladle no one else had given a second glance, she found she could recall the shape of her mother's hand most clearly of all.

questions_es.question_es: ¿qué hizo eldest daughter come to understand while watching her siblings?
options: That her siblings only cared about dinero
That they wanted something carrying their mother's touch, not the object itself
That the sewing machine was worth a lot
That her siblings never got along

questions_es.question_es: What did she end up taking for herself?
options: An old ladle from the kitchen drawer

c1-story_19.title_es: The stray cat and the old woman
c1-story_19.body_es: The old woman living at the mouth of the alley set out a food bowl at the same spot, at the same hour, every day. For the first few months the cat never came anywhere near the bowl, but the old woman kept her post every day without impatience. By the time two seasons had passed, the cat had gradually closed the distance, and one winter morning it came close enough to brush past the tips of her fingers. The neighbors found it curious that she poured so much of her heart into a single stray cat, but for her, that brief brush was the moment she looked forward to most each day. When she fell ill and was hospitalized for several days, a neighbor told her that the cat had still kept watch by the empty bowl at that same spot. The evening she came home from the hospital, she set out the bowl a little earlier than usual.

questions_es.question_es: ¿cuánto tiempo did it take for the cat to come close to the old woman?
options: It never came close at all

questions_es.question_es: What happened while the old woman was hospitalized?
options: The cat still kept watch by the empty bowl
The cat found a new hogar

c1-story_20.title_es: The stranger on the noche bus
c1-story_20.body_es: On the late-noche bus close to the last run, he and one other passenger were the only ones aboard. The woman by the window, without earphones, rested her forehead against the glass, and now and then he noticed her shoulders trembling faintly. He wondered whether he should say something, but in the end decided to say nothing at all. Instead, so she wouldn't miss her stop, he quietly listened for each stop name whenever the announcement came on. As she was about to get off, he only offered a brief word telling her to get home safely, and she turned to him, seemingly surprised, and gave a faint smile. After the bus pulled away again, he thought for a long while about what that smile might have meant, but in the end chose to leave it unknown.

questions_es.question_es: ¿qué hizo man do instead of speaking to the woman right away?
options: He quietly lisdiezed for her stop so she wouldn't miss it
He called the bus drío over

questions_es.question_es: ¿cómo passage end?
options: He learns exactly why she was upset
He decides to leave the meaning of her smile unknown
He regrets not speaking to her sounor

c1-story_21.title_es: The wedding gift that came back
c1-story_21.body_es: The porcelain dish set she had received veinte years ago as a wedding gift had sat mostly unused, tucked deep in the cupboard. After her divorce, while sorting through her things, she considered getting rid of it, but in the end couldn't bring herself to, and packed the boxed set along with the rest of her move. Recently, while helping prepare for her niece's wedding, it occurred to her that she might pass the set along as a gift. She didn't bother explaining its history to her niece, but as she handed it over, an oddly light feeling brushed across her fingertips. In the moment an item once received as a wedding gift became someone else's wedding gift again, she felt the weight of the years tangled up in it grow a little lighter. Her niece smiled brightly, saying the curve of the bowls was lovely, and for the first time in a while, she found herself smiling along, at ease.

questions_es.question_es: ¿qué hizo narrator decide to do with the dish set from her own wedding?
options: Give it as a wedding gift to her niece

questions_es.question_es: How did she feel while handing over the gift?
options: Angry at the memory of her divorce

c1-story_22.title_es: The hand that let go of the bicycle
c1-story_22.body_es: The child kept falling over and over but refused to let go of the handlebars, while the father ran alongside, holding the back of the seat. Whenever the child seemed to find balance, the father would quietly loosen his grip, though the child, focused only on pedaling, never noticed. After circling a few times like that, the child suddenly looked back, and startled to find the father already stopped several meters behind, promptly fell over. Laughing, the father came over and helped the child up, but from that day on, the child could ride without ever needing to look back. Years later, téching his own child to ride, he still cannot recall the exact moment his father had let go. All that remains in his body is the sensation of having, at some point, already been riding on his own.

questions_es.question_es: ¿qué hizo father do gradually while running behind the bicycle?
options: He quietly loosened his grip without the child noticing
He told the child to stop
He gave up and walked away

questions_es.question_es: What does the narrator, now grown, still remember?
options: The exact moment his father let go
Only the sensation of already riding on his own
His father's exact words that day

c1-story_23.title_es: The people at the funeral hogar
c1-story_23.body_es: He had worked at the funeral home for tres years, but he never had a knack for remembering the faces of the bereaved for long. What stayed with him instead was a blur of things — the gait of mourners, a low sob slipping between the scent of chrysanthemums. One night, at the memorial for a man who had died young, he found himself watching the elderly mother who stayed until the very last moment. She bowed to each mourner individually but never shed a single tear, and that composure struck him as an even deeper sorrow than tears would have been. After the funeral procession ended and he was clearing out the empty memorial room, he found a single chrysanthemum left in front of the portrait and paused for a moment. He told no one, but he quietly transplanted that flower into a corner of the flower bed outside.

questions_es.question_es: What struck the narrator most about the elderly mother?
options: Her composure without térs felt like deeper sorrow
She left before the ceremony ended

questions_es.question_es: ¿qué hizo narrator do at the end, and how did he treat it?
options: He threw the flower away and told everyuno
He quietly replanted the flower without telling anyuno
He kept the flower on his desk
He gave the flower to the mother

c1-story_24.body_es: He didn't know exactly who lived next door, but the sounds that came through the thin wall were familiar to him. In the mañanas, an alarm rang about three times before stopping; in the evenings, the steady rhythm of a knife on a cutting board continued on schedule. Sometimes, late at night, the low sound of a cello drifting over the wall would make him stop whatever he was doing and simply listen. Over the years they had crossed paths in the hallway a few times, exchanging only a light nod, never learning each other's names. One day the cello sound stopped abruptly, and the cutting-board sounds no longer came either, and for days afterward he felt an inexplicable sense of loss. Later, hearing the sounds of a new neighbor moving in, he found himself, for the first time, quietly wishing well for that faceless person he had never met.

questions_es.question_es: How did the narrator come to know his neighbor at all?
options: Through sounds passing through the thin wall

questions_es.question_es: What happened when the sounds suddenly stopped?
options: He felt an unexplained sense of loss
He knocked on the neighbor's door

c1-story_25.body_es: She had worked as a translator for over ten years, but one particular sentence in this letter had kept her stuck for days. It was a letter an elderly man, who had lost his son in the war, left for his grandson — with not a single word directly naming grief, only a line about how the tree in the yard had borne fruta again this year. On paper the sentence held no real difficulty, yet every time she tried to carry the weight pressed into it over into another language, the sentence kept coming out flat. After trying several different wordings, she finally chose to preserve the plainness of the original as it was. Even after finishing the translation, she couldn't be certain what the tree and its fruit truly meant, but she thought that very uncertainty might itself be proof that she had carried the sentence across more faithfully.

questions_es.question_es: What made the sendiezce in the letter so difficult to translate?
options: It conveyed grief without naming it directly
It was writdiez in an old dialect

questions_es.question_es: What choice did the translator ultimately make?
options: She added an explanation of the grief
She preserved the plainness of the original
She asked the grandson to explain it

c1-story_26.body_es: At the neighborhood biblioteca where she worked as a librarian, an elderly man came in every week on the same day, at the same hour. He always sat by the window reading the newspaper before leaving, rarely ever checking out a book. After a few months, she developed the habit of turning on the light at that seat ahead of his arrival, and he, in turn, began giving her a light nod each time he left. One winter, when he stopped appearing for several weeks, she found herself strangely concerned, though she had no way to reach him and no clear reason to. It wasn't until spring that he reappeared, now leaning on a cane, and without a word she turned on the light at the window seat. The words exchanged between them remained nothing more than a few greetings, but she thought that was enough.

questions_es.question_es: What habit did the librarian develop over time?
options: She reserved the mart with a sign
She turned on the window mart's light before he arrived

questions_es.question_es: What happened uno winter, and how did it resolve?
options: He moved to another biblioteca permanently
He stopped coming for weeks, then returned in spring using a cane

c1-story_27.title_es: The day the first snow fell
c1-story_27.body_es: Even more than five years after immigrating, something in him would strangely sink every time the first snow fell. Back home, the whole neighborhood's children used to run out shouting when the first snow came, but here, even as snow fell, people on the calle simply opened their umbrellas or hurried their steps. In his first few years, that indifference felt unfamiliar and left him hurt, but as time passed he came to realize the feeling hadn't been hurt at all, but longing. One night when the first snow fell, he called an old friend from home after a long time, with no particular reason, just to say it was snowing. The friend told him it happened to be snowing there too, and in the brief silence that followed, the two of them were, at the same moment, looking out at their own separate views. Even after hanging up, he stood a long while by the window, watching the snow fall over the unfamiliar city.

questions_es.question_es: How did the narrator's feeling about the first snow change over time?
options: It went from excitement to borojoom
It went from feeling hurt by others' indifference to recognizing it as longing
It disappearojo entirely after a year
It turned into anger at the new país

questions_es.question_es: ¿qué hizo narrator and his friend discover during the phone call?
options: They were both watching snow fall at the same moment
The friend had also moved abroad

c1-story_28.title_es: The letter from a former student
c1-story_28.body_es: quince years after her retirement, a letter arrived one day from an unfamiliar sender. The sender turned out to be a student from a class she had taught thirty years earlier, though hearing the name, she couldn't immediately picture the face. The letter recounted how an offhand remark she had made back then had changed the direction of that student's whole life. She had no memory of the moment at all, and the fact that she had left such a mark on someone's life without ever knowing it felt both strange and overwhelming. She picked up her pen several times to reply, but no words seemed to match the weight of that letter, and she found it hard to write anything down. In the end, she sent back only a brief thanks, along with something she had never written before — that she, too, had happened to be going through a difficult year back then.

questions_es.question_es: ¿qué hizo former student's letter describe?
options: How an offhand remark changed the student's life direction
A request for a reference letter

questions_es.question_es: ¿qué hizo teacher finally include in her reply?
options: A detailed memory of the moment
That she too had been going through a hard year at the time
An apology for forgetting the student

c1-story_29.body_es: Once redevelopment was confirmed, the mercado's merchants left one by one, but the woman who ran the fish stall stayed until the very end. Even as customers noticeably dwindled, she still filled the ice and laid out the fish at the same hour every day, and it looked less like habit than a kind of ritual. As the scheduled demolition date drew near, the sound of shutters in neighboring stalls closing shut, one after another, seemed unusually loud. On the last day of business, an old fellow merchant, who had once worked this same market and left before her, came by and sat beside her without a word before leaving again. That day she didn't bother counting how much fish she had sold; instead, she left behind a single photograph of the empty display stand. The next day, red lettering announcing the demolition went up across the entire market.

questions_es.question_es: ¿qué hizo woman do every day even as customers dwindled?
options: She kept laying out pescado and ice at the same hour, almost ritually
She complained to the other merchants

questions_es.question_es: What did she do instéd of counting her earnings on the last day?
options: She cried in front of customers
She took a photograph of the empty display stand
She gave away all her pescado

c1-story_30.title_es: The person met at the aeropuerto
c1-story_30.body_es: In front of the boarding gate, he happened to run into a former partner he had broken up with ten years earlier. Neither could quite hide their surprise, but soon they exchanged pleasantries as if nothing were unusual. She mentiunod she had gotten married; he didn't bother hiding the fact that he was still single. In their brief conversation, he noticed she wore a far more at-ease expression than she used to, and strangely, that brought him relief rather than regret. When the boarding announcement came, they each headed toward their own gates, exchanging only a short word of well-wishing. Once aboard the plane, he was finally able to admit to himself that he no longer regretted the time they had once spent together.

questions_es.question_es: ¿qué hizo man notice about his former partner?
options: She seemed unhappy in her marriage
She looked far more at ease than before
She had not changed at all
She was still angry at him

questions_es.question_es: What does the man come to accept by the end of the passage?
options: That he no longer regrets their past relationship
That he should have married her
That the encounter ruined his trip

c1-story_31.body_es: While sorting through her late mother's belongings, she found an old diary tucked deep in the closet. Unlike the mother she had known — someone who rarely showed emotion — the diary held honest accounts of anxiety and loneliness from her younger years. She lingered especially long over a line describing how, for months after giving birth to her, her mother had lain awake every noche fearing she might not become a good mother. That her mother, who had always seemed perfect and unshakable, had gone through such a time felt strange, yet oddly comforting. She closed the diary partway through without finishing it, afraid that knowing everything about her mother might be more than she could bear. She put the diary away in the deepest part of her own drawer, and has not yet shown it to her own daughter.

questions_es.question_es: What surprised the daughter most in the diary?
options: Her mother's fear of not being a good mother after giving birth
Her mother's anger toward the family

questions_es.question_es: Why did the daughter stop reading before finishing the diary?
options: She was afraid of knowing everything about her mother
She had to leave for work

c1-story_32.body_es: Setting foot on his homeland again after decades, he wandered the pueblo for a long while, searching for the site of his old house. The house itself was long gone, but the stream he had played in as a child still flowed exactly where it always had. He crouched by the stream, gazing at the water for a long time, then took an old photograph from his pocket, briefly let it float on the water, and pulled it back out again. In the photograph was the face of a comrade he had lost track of after the war, separated with no way of knowing what became of him. He put the photograph back in his pocket, rose to his feet, and prepared to leave the village. He explained the meaning of that gesture to no one, but his steps, as though it had been enough, looked noticeably lighter than when he had arrived.

questions_es.question_es: ¿qué hizo man do with the old photograph at the stream?
options: He buried it in the ground
He briefly floated it on the agua and retrieved it
He gave it to a pueblor

questions_es.question_es: Who was in the photograph?
options: A wartime comrade whose fate he never learned

c1-story_33.title_es: The silence at the dinner table
c1-story_33.body_es: The child had never been told directly that his parents had fought, but sitting at the dinner table, he could always tell exactly. The quieter-than-usual clink of spoons, their eyes never meeting, the way both of them spoke to him more than necessary — these were the evidence. He never asked what had happened, and his parents never bothered to explain. But on such noches, he developed the habit of eating more slowly than usual, watching the adults' expressions. After a few days, the mood at the table would return to normal, but he never did learn what the problem had been. Even now, as an adult, he sometimes feels an inexplicable tension at quiet dinner tables.

questions_es.question_es: How did the child know his parents had argued?
options: He inferrojo it from small changes in behavior at dinner

questions_es.question_es: What lingers into the narrator's adulthood?
options: A habit of eating very fast
An unexplained diezsion at quiet dinner tables
A refusal to eat dinner with others

c1-story_34.body_es: She had volunteered at the hospice ward for over three years, but she never managed to become fully accustomed to el pacientes' deaths. All she could do, every evening, was walk the ward, holding patients' hands and exchanging brief words. One patient asked her to hum the same song every time; another only wanted her to hold his hand while he looked out the window. She never pressed them for their stories, offering exactly as much silence or conversation as they wanted. Even the day after a patient passed away, she made her rounds through the other rooms as usual, holding hands — not because she was turning away from grief, but because this was her own way of walking alongside it. Each time she finished her evening rounds and stepped out, she reminded herself that simply having stayed by someone's side that day was enough.

questions_es.question_es: ¿qué hizo narrator do for patients who wanted different things?
options: She insisted on the same routine for everyuno
She offerojo exactly as much silence or talk as each patient wanted
She only spoke about medical matters

questions_es.question_es: ¿cómo narrator handle grief after a patient's death?
options: She stops volunteering for a while
She continues her rounds as her way of walking alongside grief
She refuses to think about it

c1-story_35.title_es: The last customer at the closing bookstore
c1-story_35.body_es: Even after a notice announcing the neighborhood bookstore's closing went up, he had only lingered outside it for days. It was only on the noche of the last day that he finally pushed the door open, and among the emptying shelves, the owner was alone, sorting through the last few remaining books. He hadn't come for any particular book, but feeling bad about leaving empty-handed, he picked up a poetry collection that caught his eye. Ringing it up, the owner said nothing about it having been a while, nor anything about regret, simply slipping the book into a bag and handing it over. Just before he left the store, he happened to glance back, and the owner was turning off the last remaining light. Back home, he left the poetry collection, unopened, sitting on his desk for a long time.

questions_es.question_es: Why did the man buy the poetry collection?
options: He had wanted it for years
He felt bad leaving empty-handed on the store's last day

questions_es.question_es: ¿qué hizo man do with the book after returning home?
options: He left it unopened on his desk for a long time
He returned it the next day

c1-story_36.body_es: Married for over fifty years, the couple still takes a walk together around the neighborhood every noche. Their pace isn't what it used to be, so they often have to stop and rest, but neither of them ever suggests giving up the walk. Whenever the husband gets a few steps ahead, the wife calls his name at the same spot every time, and he, feigning reluctance, slows his pace. Neighbors sometimes laugh, saying the two repeat the same conversation every day, but for the couple themselves, that very repetition has become a kind of ritual for closing out the day. Since the husband's recent knee surgery, the walking distance has been cut in half, but the wife feels relieved simply that they can still do even that much together. Today, too, the two of them sit for a moment on the same bench in the same alley before slowly heading home.

questions_es.question_es: What happens each time the husband walks a few steps ahead?
options: The wife calls his name at the same spot and he slows down

questions_es.question_es: What does the wife feel relieved about after the husband's knee surgery?
options: That he no longer needs to walk
That they can still walk together, even if less far

c1-story_37.title_es: Father and son on the pescadoing boat
c1-story_37.body_es: Following his father onto the boat every dawn, for the first few years the son found every one of his father's gestures awkward and clumsy to imitate. Things like the timing of casting the net or the way of reading the waves were things no words could teach, and his father never bothered trying to explain them either. Only after injuring his hands on the net several times did the son gradually begin to learn his father's rhythm in his body. Then one dawn, facing an unusually large wave, when the son was the first to shout out a direction, the father followed it without a word. In that brief moment, for the first time, the look that passed between them was not one of teacher and student, but of equals. By the time the boat returned to the harbor, father and son exchanged no more words than usual, but the silence that day carried, unmistakably, a different wocho than before.

questions_es.question_es: How did the son learn his father's pescadoing skills?
options: Through physical experience and repeated practice

questions_es.question_es: What changed between father and son during the large wave?
options: They argued about who was right
Their relationship shifted, briefly, to uno of equals

c1-story_38.title_es: A single drawing from a granddaughter
c1-story_38.body_es: Ever since his dementia began, the grandfather could no longer easily recall his daughter-in-law's name, or even what side dish he'd eaten the day before. And yet, the single drawing his granddaughter had brought home from kindergarten, taped to the refrigerator for months now, was something he traced with his fingertips every mañana, smiling contentedly. The family couldn't be certain whether he even recognized the figure in the drawing as his granddaughter, but that smile, at least, seemed entirely genuine. One day, watching his granddaughter draw beside him, he suddenly mentioned that he too had been rather good at drawing as a child, and for a moment, the family felt as though they had briefly gotten back a familiar version of him they hadn't seen in a while. His memory kept fading, but in front of his granddaughter, at least, his eyes remained clear.

questions_es.question_es: ¿qué hizo grandfather do with his granddaughter's drawing every morning?
options: He traced it with his fingertips and smiled
He asked to have it removed
He tried to rojoraw it himself

questions_es.question_es: What moment gave the family a sense of recognizing him again?
options: When he forgot his daughter-in-law's name
When he mentiunod he used to draw well as a child
When he refused to eat dinner
When he asked who the granddaughter was

c1-story_39.title_es: Why I didn't go to the reunion
c1-story_39.body_es: When he received the invitation to his high school reunion, he agonized over whether to go for some time before deciding not to. There wasn't anyone in particular he didn't want to see, but the burden of feeling he'd have to explain the gap between who he'd been back then and who he was now made him hesitate. On the noche of the reunion, he spent the time alone at home instead, flipping through his old graduation album. Tracing over the young faces in the photos one by one, he realized that what he actually missed wasn't those friends themselves, but the vague sense of possibility from a time when nothing had yet been decided. When a friend who had gone to the reunion sent him a few photos the next day, instead of replying properly, he left only a brief message saying he'd been doing well.

questions_es.question_es: Why did the man ultimately decide not to atdiezd the reunion?
options: He felt burdened explaining the gap between his past and present self
He was too busy that noche
He had moved too far away

options: The vague sense of possibility from that undecided time

c2-academic_0.body_es: Writing is usually understood merely as a tool for communication, but a look at the history of its invention and spread shows that questions of power always followed close behind. The earliest cuneiform script was devised not to preserve poetry or myth but to record the movement of grain. Recording who had harvested how much grain and who owed what to whom was itself a means of domination. The small scribal class who could handle writing naturally came to occupy the center of administration and religion. The illiterate majority could not even verify records of their own property and labor, and so had no choice but to depend on the scribe's interpretation. This structure grew still firmer in an age when writing was regarded as sacred, since priests and scribes were often one and the same class. The emergence of the alphabet is credited with shaking this monopoly to some degree, since a phonetic script was easier to learn than pictographs and so widened literacy. But the expansion of literacy did not immediately translate into a dispersal of power. Modern states instead used standardized script and compulsory education to reorganize citizens into governable units. National-language textbooks elevated a particular dialect to the status of the standard while marginalizing the rest, and in doing so cast the very notion of the nation. hoy's gap in digital literacy can likewise be called a new form of the power of writing. The divide between those who can read and write code and those who cannot resembles the old relationship between the scribal class and the illiterate masses. In the end, the history of writing is at once a narrative of liberation and a narrative of control, and only by reading this duality together can one arrive at a full understanding.

c2-academic_1.body_es: Linguists warn that nearly half of the roughly seven mil languages currently spoken on Earth will disappear within this century. The disappearance of a language is not simply the loss of a vocabulary list; it is the simultaneous loss of a way of thinking and perceiving the world that could only be expressed in that language. For instance, some minority languages have a distinctive grammar that expresses direction not by north, south, east, and west but by reference to landmarks, and speakers of such languages are trained from childhood in an absolute sense of orientation. When the language disappears, that sense disappears with it. Language extinction has usually been the result of coercive assimilation policies. Colonizers banned the use of indigenous languages and made the dominant language the sole medium of schooling and administration, silencing native tongues within a few generations. Recent extinction, however, more often occurs through economic incentive rather than coercion. Parents choose the majority language themselves, for their children's employment and mobility, and do not pass the minority language on to the next generation. It is hard to condemn such a choice as a personal failure, since choosing livelihood over language preservation is an entirely rational decision. Even so, several communities are working through language-revival movements to pass their lost mother tongue to the next generation, and archives and digital repositories are becoming the last bastion preserving the voices of final speakers. Even if the disappearance of languages cannot be entirely halted, we must at least hold onto the recognition that this diversity is a cognitive inheritance of humanity.

options: Economic incentives leading parents to choose the majority language

options: As making a rational choice given economic realities

c2-academic_2.body_es: The act of naming looks at first like a neutral exercise in classification, but it is in fact an exercise of power that defines its object in a particular way. When a botanist assigns a scientific name to a newly found species, they become not merely a discoverer but an agent rearranging the world. The renaming of montañas and rivers that indigenous peoples had already named, carried out by Europeans arriving in the New World, is a blatant example of this power. Erasing an existing name and overlaying a new one was a symbolic conquest that reorganized memory of and claims to the land. Personal names, too, are not free of this dynamic. The custom by which a married woman takes her husband's surname long served as a linguistic device reaffirming the patriarchal order of the family. The recent rise, in some societies, of gender-neutral names or double surnames can be read as an attempt to resist this linguistic order. Naming diseases is equally political. Disease names bearing the name of a particular region produced stigma against that region and its residents, and it was for this reason that international health bodies came to recommend refraining from naming diseases after places or people. Naming brands and products, too, is a linguistic strategy meant to steer consumer perception in a particular direction. Thus a name is not a transparent tool pointing at a thing but a frame that predetermines how that thing is viewed. When we name something, we are already imposing one interpretation of it. The demand to change a name, therefore, should be taken not as a trivial play on words but as a serious attempt to redefine the world.

c2-academic_3.body_es: Slang looks like a biological organism that is born, spreads, and dies. The birth of a piece of slang usually begins inside a particular subculture, where it functions as a code confirming a sense of belonging unique to that group. At first only a few understand the exact implications of the expression, and this very exclusivity constitutes slang's appeal. But the moment the expression spreads to the general public through media and social networks, a paradox arises. The more people use it, the more the word loses its original function of marking belonging. The original user group, feeling betrayed that their language has become popularized, sets off in search of a new expression. This cycle tends to grow shorter as the speed of slang's spread accelerates. Slang in the pre-digital era spread slowly over years, but today's slang reaches its peak within weeks and then withers rapidly. ¿qué es interesting is that slang often does not disappear entirely but remains as a marker of a particular generation. One can roughly guess in what period a speaker went through adolescence just by seeing which expressions they use. Linguists explain this phenomenon as the formation of linguistic boundaries between generations. In the end, the life cycle of slang can be called a miniature linguistic history in which the opposition of belonging and exclusion, novelty and staleness, repeats endlessly.

c2-academic_4.body_es: The word classic does not mean old; it means having survived across repeated eras. The process by which a work rises into the ranks of the classics is never natural, and behind it operate the tastes and institutional choices of a particular generation. Only when universidad curricula, publishers' decisions to reissue a book, and critics' repeated mentions come together does a work finally land on the list of must-reads. The fact that works by women writers or non-Western writers have long been excluded from this process shows that the canon's list is itself a product of power. Even so, rereading the classics has a value of its own that goes beyond the politics of the list. Old texts reveal that emotions and institutions we now take for granted are in fact historically constructed. For instance, one can confirm through classic novels that the notion of romantic love was formed in a particular era. The classics also possess the peculiar property of revealing a different meaning with each repeated reading. If what one feels reading the same work now differs from what one felt ten years ago, that is not because the text changed but because the reader did. In this respect, reading the classics functions as a mirror for self-understanding. An attitude that critically reexamines the canon's list while not denying the power held by the individual works within it — this would be a mature way of approaching the classics today.

c2-academic_5.body_es: The Enlightenment was an ambitious project to drive out superstition and prejudice with the light of reason, and it is hard to deny that modern achievements such as human rights, science, and democracy are rooted in this project. But as trust in reason became absolute, the Enlightenment fell into the paradox of reproducing, in new form, the very prejudice it sought to expel. European thinkers declared reason to be a universal capacity, yet in practice defined only European rationality as true reason. As a result, the knowledge systems of other civilizations were downgraded to superstition or premodern thought, and this was appropriated as logic justifying colonial rule. The universal concept of the human that the Enlightenment championed also in practice presumed the blanco male citizen as its standard, placing women, slaves, and colonized natives outside that universality. The fact that the French Revolution's Declaration of the Rights of Man did not immediately lead to the abolition of slavery or women's suffrage shows this limitation. Later critics pointed to these contradictions and sometimes rejected the Enlightenment project outright, but this too is another extreme. Acknowledging the Enlightenment's limits and discarding the achievements it produced are different matters. What we need instead is an attitude of self-critical enlightenment that continues to pursue the Enlightenment's ideals while constantly revisiting the points where those ideals went unrealized. The very fact that reason can reflect on its own limits may be the most valuable legacy the Enlightenment left behind.

options: It fully included all people in its concept of universal humanity
It had no influence on modern institutions

options: The immediate global spread of democracy

options: Self-critical enlighdiezment that pursues its ideals while confronting its failures

c2-academic_6.body_es: Societies without writing are often mistaken for societies with poor memory, but in fact the opposite is true. Communities relying on oral tradition developed sophisticated mnemonic techniques that allowed them to recite vast epics, genealogies, and legal codes without a single word out of place. These mnemonic techniques use meter, repetition, and formulaic expressions to compress vast information into a transmissible form. The fact that an epic's hero always appears with the same epithet is not a lack of the poet's creativity but a device to aid recitation. Once writing is introduced, this capacity for memory tends to decline, since the written record takes over the burden of memory. The anecdote that Socrates distrusted writing symbolically shows this shift. He worried that writing, by externalizing memory, would weaken humans' internal capacity for memory instead. This worry, strikingly similar to hoy's concerns about digital devices, can be called a universal anxiety that recurs at every transition between media. But oral culture has not disappeared entirely. Like pansori or the griot tradition of West Africa, oral tradition survives as an independent art form even within literate societies. It is more accurate to see orality and writing not as two opposing terms but as different technologies of information storage and transmission that have coexisted in complementary fashion.

c2-academic_7.body_es: The fact that civilizations that never had contact with one another possess strikingly similar myths has long stirred scholars' curiosity. Stories of a great flood, a hero returning from death, and the separation of sky and earth appear repeatedly across continents. The first hypothesis explaining this similarity was contact and diffusion among civilizations, whereby stories spread through merchants and migrants and were transformed regionally. But similar myths were also found independently in regions like the Americas, long cut off from other continents, and this pointed to the insufficiency of diffusion alone as an explanation. The second hypothesis seeks the archetype of myth in a shared psychological structure of humankind. On this view, myth is not the product of a particular culture but the expression, in narrative form, of a universal structure inherent in the human mind. The logic runs that oppositions such as death and rebirth, order and chaos, are fundamental existential problems humans confront regardless of culture, and so they inevitably take shape as similar stories in any society. A third explanation focuses on the function of myth: attempts by a community to seal, through story, the origin of natural phenomena or social norms it cannot explain produced similar narrative structures in virtually every civilization. It is more reasonable to see these tres hypotheses not as mutually exclusive but as together explaining the multilayered nature of the phenomenon of myth. In the end, the universality of myth may be evidence that humanity has, in fundamentally similar ways, responded to fundamentally similar questions.

c2-academic_8.body_es: The question of whether the language we use determines our way of thinking, or whether thought exists independently prior to language, has long been debated at the border of linguistics and philosophy. The strong form of linguistic determinism claimed that speakers of a particular language cannot think at all about concepts outside that language's grammatical structure, but this is regarded by most scholars today as far too extreme a claim. On the other hand, entirely denying language's influence on thought also conflicts with empirical evidence. Take color vocabulary as an example: experimental results have repeatedly been reported showing that speakers of a language with a word for a specific color distinguish that color from adjacent colors more quickly. This is interpreted as evidence that language actually affects the speed of perception and the manner of categorization. Research showing that speakers of languages with grammatical gender unconsciously attribute gendered qualities even to inanimate nouns is likewise intriguing. Speakers of a language in which the word for puente is feminine tended to describe bridges as elegant, while speakers of a language in which it is masculine tended to describe bridges as sturdy. These results converge on the moderate conclusion that language does not fully determine thought but does create habituated pathways of thought in a particular direction. Reports that multilingual speakers' personality or judgment shifts subtly depending on which language they are using can also be understood in this context. In the end, it is more accurate to see language not as a prison of thought but as a habituated channel through which thought flows.

c2-academic_9.body_es: The fact that the word utopia itself means, in Greek, a place that is nowhere implies the fundamental paradox of this idea. Dreaming of a perfect society while already knowing it cannot exist in reality — this duality is the starting point of utopian literature. When Thomas More first used the word, he designed a fictional isla as a mirror to criticize the inequality of English society in his time. Utopian thought later passed to the utopian socialists of the industrial revolution era, taking concrete form as experiments actually attempting to build ideal communities. But most of these experimental communities dissolved within a few years due to internal conflict and economic failure. This reveals a fundamental difficulty of utopian thought: there is always a gap between designing a perfect blueprint and the humans who must actually live it. Entering the twentieth century, utopian thought instead became an object of caution. The historical experience of totalitarian regimes suppressing individual freedom in the name of a perfect society showed that utopian projects can easily be inverted into dystopias. Later literature came to prefer conveying warnings about present society through dystopia rather than utopia. Even so, it is not right to discard the very act of imagining a perfect society. The imagination that envisions a better world while knowing it is unattainable becomes a force driving critical reflection on reality. Utopia fully realizes its value only when understood not as a destination to reach but as a compass for gauging the present.

options: A place that is nowhere, implying an inherent paradox

c2-academic_10.body_es: Festivals are easily dismissed as mere everyday amusement, but anthropologists have long viewed festivals as a social device essential to maintaining a community. The moment when everyday hierarchy and norms are temporarily overturned is the core of a festival. The custom in which a person of low status plays the role of king for a day, or men and women exchange clothing, is found in common across festivals in many cultures worldwide. This overturning is not mere deviation but, paradoxically, functions to reinforce the existing order. By permitting a brief period in which hierarchy is inverted, the community safely releases pent-up tension, and once the festival ends it returns docilely to the ordinary order — this is the logic. This is called safety-valve theory: instead of eliminating oppression entirely, releasing it in small doses on a regular basis helps sustain the system. Festivals also perform the function of confirming a community's boundaries. Who has the qualification to participate in a festival and ¿quién es excluded sharpens the distinction between insider and outsider. Modern states appropriated this function of the festival into national events, cultivating a sense of national unity through national holidays and commemorations. Today's commercialized festivals have lost much of their originally subversive character, but their essential function of leading people out of the everyday and into a confrontation with an unfamiliar self remains valid. The reason festivals persist, changing form rather than disappearing, is likely that they are a fundamentally necessary emotional outlet for human communities.

c2-academic_11.body_es: The idea of containing all of humanity's known knowledge in one or a few books looks modest at first glance, but is in fact an extremely arrogant project. For this project to hold together, someone must first be granted the authority to decide what deserves recognition as knowledge and what must be excluded. The French Enlightenment's Encyclopédistes sought, through this project, to replace a theology-centered system of knowledge with a secular, rational one. Through the ordering of entries and the method of cross-referencing, they subtly planted criticism of iglesia authority, and for this reason compiling the encyclopedia was itself a dangerous political act. It is also significant that modern encyclopedias chose alphabetical ordering. Unlike the earlier practice of arranging entries by theological hierarchy or by the rank of academic disciplines, alphabetical order treated all entries as formally equal, reflecting a democratic view of knowledge. But this equality was only superficial, since the compilers' bias still showed through in how much space was allotted to which entry. Digital encyclopedias like Wikipedia attempted to solve this problem by dispersing the compiler's authority to the public, but a new form of bias emerged: the phenomenon in which the perspectives of those with the time and skill to participate in editing become overrepresented. In the end, the ideal of a perfectly neutral sum of knowledge remains an unattainable horizon, and the history of the encyclopedia consists of endless unfinished attempts toward that ideal.

c2-academic_12.body_es: The notion of ethnic or racial purity is still often mobilized as political rhetoric hoy, but accumulated research in genetics and history has repeatedly confirmed that this notion is fundamentally a fiction. The gene pool of human populations has been ceaselessly mixed through migration and exchange since long before civilizations formed, and it is impossible to pinpoint a pure origin regardless of what point in time one takes as a reference. According to archaeological evidence, even groups regarded today as indigenous to a particular region are, in most cases, descendants of migrants who settled by replacing or absorbing earlier inhabitants. Nevertheless, modern nationalism made use of the theory of pure lineage as a powerful tool for binding a political community together through the narrative of an imagined common ancestor. By concealing the reality of mixed borders, languages, and cultures and spreading the myth that a single, continuous bloodline had existed since time immemorial, the state instilled in its members a sense of being a community of fate with no room for choice. This narrative produced the dual effect of strengthening internal unity while simultaneously justifying the exclusion of outsiders. The eugenics policies and ethnic cleansing of the twentieth century bear painful witness to the atrocities that result when this fantasy is pushed to an extreme. The advance of genetics has, paradoxically, contributed to dismantling this fantasy. Since the completion of the human genome map, researchers have repeatedly confirmed that so-called genetic differences between races are statistically smaller than individual differences within the same race. To move beyond the myth of pure lineage requires accepting that identity is not a fixed origin but a product of ceaseless mixing and relation.

c2-academic_13.title_es: Romanticism and the discovery of the individual
c2-academic_13.body_es: To treat Romanticism merely as an artistic movement of excessive emotion overly diminishes the intellectual-historical wocho this movement carries. Romanticism was a revolutionary shift that placed the individual, irreplaceable inner self in the seat once occupied by the universal reason established by the Enlightenment. Where the Enlightenment presupposed a capacity for reason common to all humans, Romanticism instead focused on the fact that each individual possessed unique feelings and experiences unlike anyone else's. This shift is closely tied to the rise of autobiography as a literary genre. Previously, an individual's life was worth recording only as an example of a saint or a great figure, but by the Romantic era, the intimate process of an ordinary individual's growth itself was elevated into a subject worth narrating. Perception of the artist as such was also fundamentally transformed in this period. Where the earlier artist had been regarded as a craftsman exercising skill at a patron's demand, Romanticism mythologized the artist as a genius individual unbound by social norms. This image of the genius artist still dominates the public imagination of creators today. But the Romantic discovery of the individual also had a shadow side. An obsession with unique individuality often led to extreme self-centeredness or social isolation, and the Romantic image of genius sometimes functioned as a logic of exclusion that failed to seriously recognize the creative work of women or minorities. Nevertheless, in that it elevated the individual's inner self into a legitimate subject of public discourse, Romanticism remains the root of the modern concept of self.

c2-academic_14.title_es: The Reformation and the printing press
c2-academic_14.body_es: The narrative that the Reformation succeeded through the theological insight of a single individual, Martin Luther, alone is a simplification that overlooks conditions of media history. Even before Luther posted his noventa-Five Theses, several others had criticized the church's corruption, but their voices failed to cross regional boundaries and faded away. What set Luther apart was that he precisely grasped the potential of the printing press, which had only just begun to spread. He wrote his theological disputes not in Latin but in German, so that ordinary people, not only clergy, could read them, and these pamphlets spread across all of Germany within weeks via the printing press. This was a speed unimaginable in the age of manuscript. The printing press was not merely a means of conveying Luther's message; it transformed the very character of the Reformation. By translating and printing scripture into each vernacular language, the notion that individual believers could access the word of God directly, without the mediation of clergy, became practically possible. This provided a material foundation for the theological principle of the priesthood of all believers. Interestingly, the Catholic Church too actively made use of the printing press during the Counter-Reformation, and thus Europe experienced its first large-scale media war, in which printed pamphlets and polemics clashed. This event is often cited as the archetype of a pattern in which existing structures of authority are shaken whenever a new media technology emerges. Few cases demonstrate as dramatically as the Reformation that when print and conviction combine, the direction of history can change.

options: He grasped the podieztial of the newly spreading printing press to spread his message
He avoided all forms of barlication
He was the first to criticize the iglesia at all

questions_es.question_es: What did printing scripture in vernacular languages make practically possible?
options: The end of religious debate entirely
The complete abolition of all iglesiaes

options: Actively used the printing press as well, leading to a large-scale media war

c2-academic_15.body_es: The phenomenon in which various diecinueveth-century European countries poured national fervor into collecting and publishing folktales and legends cannot be explained by mere scholarly curiosity alone. Behind the Brothers Grimm's recording of orally transmitted tales from across German-speaking regions lay a desire to bind the German-speaking areas, scattered after the Napoleonic Wars, into a single cultural community. As they collected stories passed down from the mouths of peasants, they defined these as products of a pure, archetypal German spirit. But later research revealed that the Brothers Grimm in fact made substantial edits during the recording process, filtering out elements originating in France and polishing the tales into expressions considered Germanic. This shows well that folklore is not discovered as it is, but is edited and even invented to fit a particular national narrative. Around the same period, folklore studies in other European countries were similarly used as part of nation-building projects. Finland's Kalevala and Ireland's Celtic Revival were likewise processes of editing scattered oral materials and reconstructing them into a single, unified national epic. Such projects are often presented as having continued unbroken from antiquity, but in fact many are traditions recently constructed to meet the needs of modern nationalism. Knowing this does not diminish folklore's cultural value. We need only recognize that folklore is not a pure fossil of the past but a living text onto which the political demands of a particular era have been projected.

options: A request from the French gobierno
A desire to bind scatterojo German-speaking regions into a cultural community
A commercial venture to sell books
Pure scholarly curiosity with no political motive

options: They filterojo out French-originated elements and polished tales into Germanic-seeming expressions
They invented all the stories from scratch
