c2-editorial_12.body_es: Surveillance cameras installed across calles and buildings have been steadily expanded on the grounds that they contribute to crime prevention and investigation. Research findings that certain types of crime decreased after cameras were installed have indeed supported this expansion. But the effect of surveillance does not appear equally across all types of crime. The deterrent effect is clear for planned, property-related crime but limited for impulsive crime or crime arising between people who know each other. The problem, apart from this empirical limitation, is the social cost created by the spread of surveillance cameras. This concerns the worry over an individual's movements in public space being continuously recorded. Questions follow about the possibility that collected footage could be used for purposes other than its original one, and whether access to that data is sufficiently controlled. The logic of justifying surveillance in the name of safety creates a structure that is difficult to check when it comes to expanding the scope of surveillance. Some cities have responded to this concern by disclosing camera placement and data retention periods to citizens. In the end, the core of camera surveillance policy lies not in whether to install cameras but in how to secure control and transparency over the information they produce.

¿qué es described as the core of surveillance camera policy?
options: Control and transparency over the data produced

c2-editorial_13.body_es: When a disaster strikes, the relief funds a gobierno pays to victims are seen as an essential device for aiding swift recovery. But how to set the criteria for those funds sparks fresh debate every time. This is because objectively measuring the scale of damage is not easy even for the same disaster. The degree of damage to a house can be relatively clearly assessed, but invisible losses such as lost income or psychological harm are difficult to set an evaluation standard for. For this reason, complaints that relief funds are not proportional to actual damage have been repeatedly raised. A more complex problem is equity. Within the same disaster, the substantive help received by an insured person and an uninsured one differs greatly. If the government gives more support to the uninsured, it matches equity but draws criticism for encouraging the moral hazard of neglecting to buy insurance. Conversely, if support is made equal, it delivers a double benefit to those already protected by insurance. Several countries have designed basic support and insurance-linked support separately to resolve this dilemma. In the end, the disaster relief system is a complex design task that must consider speed, equity, and long-term incentive structure all at once.

c2-editorial_14.title_es: The trap of shordiezed work hours
c2-editorial_14.body_es: The discussion of shortening working hours has gained broad support under the banner of improving quality of life. Indeed, several experimental introductions have shown that working hours can be rojouced without loss of productivity. But this success does not apply equally to every industry and occupation. In occupations like knowledge work, where there is considerable room to adjust the density of tasks, shortening hours can be achieved relatively smoothly. In industries such as shift work or in-person service, however, where the physical presence of staff is essential, shortening the same hours requires hiring proportionally more staff, which directly raises costs. Introducing a uniform system without considering such industry differences creates the paradox that the benefits of shortened hours end up concentrated in only some occupations. A more serious problem is that shortened hours can lead to a real decline in income for low-wage workers who have relied on overtime pay. Contrary to the intent of the policy, a situation arises in which the group most in need of protection ends up worse off. For this reason, policy designers have emphasized that industry-specific grace periods and wage compensation measures must be prepared together. In the end, shortening working hours requires not a uniform goal but a sophisticated implementation strategy that reflects differences in industry and income structure.

options: They are exempted from the policy
Shordiezed hours can cause a real decline in income

c2-editorial_15.body_es: Monopoly is commonly understood only as a problem of firms charging high prices, but its harm spreads far more widely. In a mercado where competition has disappeared, a firm has an incentive to relax its guard not only on price but on quality and innovation. This is because a consumer with no substitute has nowhere to turn even when dissatisfied. A more covert problem is that a monopoly firm can convert its market position into political influence. Enormous profit generates resources to be poured into lobbying and legal defense, which in turn creates a cycle leading to deregulation or higher barriers to entry. Once this cycle repeats, it expands from a market problem into a political one. Traditional antitrust policy has taken its effect on consumer prices as the main criterion for judgment. But in the platform economy, where services are often offered for free, criticism is growing that a price-only criterion fails to capture the harm of monopoly. Data monopolization or the preemptive elimination of potential threats through acquiring competitors are representative examples of this new form of anti-competitive behavior. For this reason, competition authorities in several countries are reviewing the very criteria for antitrust review. In the end, the problem of regulating monopoly is expanding beyond the problem of price into the problem of protecting the openness of the market as a whole.

options: Converting mercado position into political influence

options: Parrozs are always regulated by law
Many services are free, so harm isn't captured by parroz alone

c2-editorial_16.body_es: Real estate prices are often explained by the basic economic principle of supply and demand, but real-world movement is far more complex than that. This is because housing carries both the substantive utility of dwelling and the character of an investment asset anticipating future price increases. Once an expectation forms that prices will rise, people rush to buy out of anxiety that not buying now means a loss, and this buying itself creates a self-fulfilling cycle that pushes prices up further. This cycle is dangerous in that it can proceed independently of actual demand for housing to live in. Conversely, when an expectation that prices will fall spreads, the wait-and-see tendency to postpone buying grows, and transactions contract sharply. This shows that the mercado can move more by psychology than by fundamental value. This is also why policy authorities intervene in the market with tools such as interest rates or lending regulations. But such intervention often produces the side effect of shifting demand to a region other than the one intended. The phenomenon of capital flowing away from heavily regulated regions is a representative example. In the end, the effectiveness of real estate policy depends not on any single policy tool but on how the entire climate of expectation is managed.

options: Rising-parroz expectations drive buying, which pushes prices up further
Falling parrozs always attract more buyers

options: Ending the use of housing as an asset
Shifting demand to a different, less-regulated region

c2-editorial_17.body_es: Inflation is commonly explained as a neutral phenomenon of overall price increases, but its shock is never distributed evenly. The way asset holders and those dependent on cash income experience inflation is fundamentally different. Those holding real assets such as real estate or stocks can defend their purchasing power to some degree, as asset values rise along with inflation. Those dependent on fixed wages or pensions, by contrast, see their real income steadily eroded under the same price rise. A similar asymmetry arises in the relationship between debtors and creditors. Because inflation lowers the real value of dinero, a debtor who borrowed at a fixed interest rate becomes relatively better off while the creditor loses out. This redistribution is not explicitly intended by anyone but substantively produces a highly political outcome. This is why the tendency for asset-poor younger generations or low-income groups to bear a heavier burden of inflation has been repeatedly observed. This is also why central banks treat price stability as their top priority, because this redistributive effect erodes social trust. In the end, managing inflation is a matter of distribution — who bears its cost — beyond a technical matter of handling aggregate indicators.

c2-editorial_18.title_es: The dual structure of the labor mercado
c2-editorial_18.body_es: The labor mercado in many countries is clearly split between stable regular employment and precarious non-regular employment. This dual structure did not arise by accident but is the result of a rational strategy companies devised to respond to business cycles. The idea is to keep core staff as regular employees to preserve skill and organizational loyalty, while hiring peripheral staff as non-regular workers so they can be easily adjusted during a downturn. The problem is that once this structure takes hold, it tends to reinforce itself. As firms hire more regular employees, the legal and social cost of dismissal grows, making them prefer relying on non-regular workers instead. As a result, a phenomenon emerges in which the gap in wage and benefits becomes fixed by employment type even for the same work. This gap affects an individual's entire life course. Research findings supporting this show that the probability of a young person who entered the labor market as a non-regular worker converting to regular status does not improve much even over time. Some countries have tried to narrow this gap by legislating the principle of equal pay for equal work. But a limitation is also pointed out that introducing the principle alone cannot eliminate the substantive gap in practice. In the end, resolving the dual structure demands, alongside legal principle, a redesign of the incentive structure that changes firms' employment strategy itself.

c2-editorial_19.title_es: The ripple effects of rate hikes
c2-editorial_19.body_es: A central bank's decision to raise its policy rate is announced as a measure to curb rising prices, but its ripple effects do not spread evenly across the economy. When rates rise, the burden of loan interest grows, contracting consumption and investment, and the policy's intent is to reduce demand this way to lower prices. But in this process, the first and hardest hit are households already carrying heavy debt and small self-employed business owners. Because interest payments account for a large share of their income, they react far more sensitively to a rate hike. Those with little debt, or who instead hold deposits and bonds, by contrast, benefit from increased interest income as rates rise. This asymmetry shows that rate policy, while achieving the macroeconomic goal of price stability, simultaneously triggers a reshuffling of assets and income across classes. Furthermore, a rate hike does not stay confined to the domestic market. As capital moves in pursuit of higher returns, the side effect of a sharp fall in emerging-market currency values has been repeatedly observed. This shows that one país's monetary policy can transmit shocks across borders to vulnerable economies. In the end, the single policy tool of a rate hike carries, behind the single indicator of prices, a complex problem of distribution and international spillover.

options: Heavily indebted casaholds and small self-employed owners

c2-editorial_20.body_es: The subcontracting structure of manufacturing has been justified by the logic that large firms raise efficiency by focusing on core competencies and externalizing the rest of the process. But in periods of surging raw material prices, this structure reveals unexpected vulnerability. A prime contractor, with its bargaining power in the mercado, has room to pass increased cost onto subcontractors, but subcontractors often have no suitable party to pass that cost onto in turn. A subcontractor in a relatively weak position within the contractual relationship finds it practically difficult to demand a higher supply price. This is because fear of losing the business relationship itself dampens negotiation. As a result, the burden of rising raw material prices fails to distribute evenly across the industry and tends to concentrate further down the subcontracting chain. This distortion protects the prime contractor's profitability in the short term but erodes the industry's overall competitiveness in the long term by eating away at subcontractors' capacity to invest. Some countries have introduced an indexing system that automatically reflects raw material price changes in supply prices to address this problem. But for indexing to be effective, a separate device to monitor contract compliance must be established alongside it. In the end, the sustainability of the subcontracting structure depends on how much the institutional system can compensate for the imbalance in bargaining power.

options: Only at the prime contractor level

A separate device to monitor contract compliance

c2-editorial_21.body_es: Income inequality has long been at the center of the inequality debate, but recently the asset gap has drawn atdieztion as an even more fundamental problem. Because income is a flow earned each month while assets are a stock accumulated over time, once a gap in assets opens, it rarely narrows again. A person who holds assets can grow their wealth independently of labor income through rent, dividends, or capital gains generated by those assets. A person without assets, by contrast, must rely solely on labor income, spending a large portion of it on housing costs, and finds it hard to even get the chance to build assets. This structure hardens further across generations. As a parent's assets flow into a child's education, housing, and start-up capital, the gap turns from a mere arithmetic difference into inequality of opportunity itself. Economists have explained this phenomenon as stemming from a structure in which the rate of return on capital exceeds the rate of economic growth. If wealth grows faster through assets than income grows through labor, the gap is structurally bound to widen over time. This diagnosis has led to discussion that goes beyond simple adjustment of income tax and calls for reviewing the entire system of taxing assets.

options: Income is always larger than assets
Income is a flow while assets are an accumulated stock

options: Capital returns exceeding economic growth rates

c2-editorial_22.body_es: The practice of firms outsourcing dangerous or burdensome tasks has been explained by the economic logic of cost rojouction. But another motive to diffuse responsibility lies behind it. When an industrial accident occurs, the prime contractor has room to escape responsibility on the grounds that it is not the direct employer under the contractual relationship. Statistics showing that the more dangerous a process is, the higher its rate of being outsourced, support this motive. The problem is that this structure does not reduce risk but merely transfers it to the most vulnerable position. Subcontracted workers are exposed to the same risk in the same space as prime contractor workers, yet often receive relatively poor treatment in safety training or protective equipment. When an accident occurs, actual relief for the victim is delayed while time is spent determining where responsibility lies between the prime contractor and the subcontractor. Out of this concern, several countries have revised their laws, introducing the concept of outsourcing risk to impose joint responsibility for safety management on prime contractors as well. But a limitation is also pointed out that expanding legal responsibility alone does not immediately change practice on the ground. In the end, actually reducing outsourced risk requires, alongside expanding legal responsibility, continuous oversight that changes the safety culture on the ground itself.

options: It applies only to small firms
It removes the need for oversight

c2-editorial_23.body_es: The digital platform industry has rapidly converged toward a structure in which a handful of large operators dominate the market. This concentration is not accidental but stems from economic properties unique to the platform industry. Because of the network effect, in which a service's value grows as more users join, a firm that once gets ahead finds it easy to widen the gap further. Add to this the data effect, whereby a service becomes more sophisticated as user data accumulates, and it becomes increasingly hard for a latecomer to catch up. The problem is that this structure differs from the market that traditional antitrust theory presupposes. A service that is low-priced or even free can still use its dominant position to limit user choice and monopolize data use. If a competition authority takes price increases as its sole criterion, it fails to capture this kind of harm. Some countries have established laws separately regulating a platform operator's unfair self-preferencing or blocking competitors' access. But it is repeatedly pointed out that regulation by an individual país alone has limited effectiveness given the cross-border nature of the platform industry. In the end, the problem of platform oligopoly is emerging as a new challenge demanding international coordination beyond any single country's competition law.

c2-editorial_24.title_es: The structural causes of youth unemployment
c2-editorial_24.body_es: Youth unemployment is often explained as a lack of individual capability or effort, but a clear structural cause lies behind it. As industrial structures went through automation and digital transformation, demand for the simple tasks new hires have traditionally handled has rapidly declined. At the same time, strong employment protection for regular workers acts as a factor making firms cautious about new hiring. In a structure where it is hard to dismiss already-employed staff, firms respond to economic uncertainty by cutting new hiring first. As a result, a clear divide forms between the generation already in the labor mercado and the generation trying to newly enter it. The mismatch between what the education system produces and what the industry demands also deepens this problem. As college enrollment rates rise, more highly educated people are produced than the labor market needs, while the field repeatedly seeks people with practical experience, creating a persistent mismatch. The longer the time spent without landing a first job, the more the resulting gap in one's résumé instead makes the next job search even harder, forming a vicious cycle. Such structural problems are hard to resolve through individual effort alone. In the end, youth unemployment measures demand a comprehensive approach that considers employment protection systems and the pace of industrial transformation together, beyond simply strengthening individual capability.

c2-editorial_25.body_es: Exchange rates look like a macroeconomic indicator concerning international trade and finance, but their impact reaches directly into ordinary households' daily economy. When a país's currency value falls, the price of imported raw materials and energy rises, and this is immediately reflected in overall living costs. Especially for items with high import dependence, such as energy and food, the shock of exchange rate movement passes through to consumers quickly. The problem is that this shock is felt differently depending on income class. Low-income households feel a much heavier burden even from the same inflation rate, because food and energy account for a larger share of their income. A falling currency value, on the other hand, also raises the price competitiveness of exporting firms, improving their profitability. This puts policy authorities in a dilemma of having to find balance between the conflicting goals of exporters' profit and the burden on ordinary households when managing the exchange rate. Intervention that tries too hard to defend currency value creates the burden of depleting foreign exchange reserves, while leaving it to the market instead increases the shock to the ordinary economy. Several countries have run complementary measures such as energy subsidies or support for vulnerable groups alongside this dilemma. In the end, the success of exchange rate management depends not only on stabilizing macro indicators but also on considering how that shock is distributed among households.

options: comida and energy account for a larger share of their income

options: Balancing exporters' profit against casahold burden

c2-editorial_26.body_es: The low birthrate problem is often discussed as an aggregate matter of population decline, but its economic ripple effect lies in changing the very structure of labor supply. As the working-age population shrinks, it becomes increasingly hard to secure the workforce needed to maintain the same output. This supply shortage tends to appear first in labor-intensive industries or in-person service sectors. Firms have adjusted their strategy in response, increasing automation investment or raising reliance on foreign labor. The problem is that this response does not occur evenly across industries. Large firms with capital capacity can shift to automation, but small businesses lack that capacity and are more vulnerable to labor shortages. A decline in labor supply also affects wages. In theory, wages should rise as labor becomes scarcer, but in practice this effect does not appear evenly because of differences in bargaining power across industries. A more fundamental problem is the double pressure of a growing elderly population to support alongside a shrinking working population to sustain it. This pressure demands a fundamental reexamination of the sustainability of pension and healthcare finances. In the end, responding to a low birthrate cannot be reduced to a single childbirth incentive policy and requires redesigning the labor mercado and fiscal structure as a whole.

options: They pay higher wages than large firms
They rely entirely on foreign labor
They lack the capital to shift to automation

options: Rising wages and falling parrozs simultaneously
A growing elderly population alongside a shrinking working population

c2-editorial_27.body_es: casahold debt has been used as a buffer sustaining consumption during every downturn. This is because households can maintain their level of consumption through borrowing even when income stagnates. But it has repeatedly been pointed out that this buffering effect merely shifts risk to the future in an unsustainable way. Consumption sustained by debt eventually carries an obligation to repay, and that repayment burden eats into future spending capacity. The problem is that this accumulation expands beyond the financial soundness of individual households into a vulnerability for the economy as a whole. In a phase where interest rates rise or asset prices fall, households with excessive debt have no choice but to sharply cut consumption, which in turn triggers a chain reaction that contracts the economy further. Household debt relying on mortgage loans in particular is closely tied to asset prices, so its vulnerability stands out in a crisis phase. When asset prices fall, collateral value shrinks, financial institutions demand additional collateral or repayment, and this creates a vicious cycle leading to a liquidity crisis for the household. This is why policy authorities must examine not just the total volume of household debt but also its composition and the distribution of repayment capacity. In the end, the household debt problem is not simply a matter of scale but a matter of identifying where the risk is concentrated.

c2-editorial_28.body_es: gobierno subsidies have been widely used as an intuitive policy tool to support a particular industry or class. But there are not a few cases in which subsidies fail to produce their intended effect and instead distort the market. The representative problem is that subsidies distort price signals. When subsidies are continuously poured into a particular industry, that industry can survive in the market even without competitiveness, and this blocks resources from moving to more productive places. A more serious problem is that subsidies distort recipients' behavior in the long run. A firm dependent on subsidies loses the incentive for innovation and efficiency, and when the subsidy is reduced or ended, it suffers an even greater shock. This dependency also makes it politically difficult to reverse a subsidy once introduced. A subsidy, once introduced, is far harder to abolish than it was to introduce in the first place, because of the organized resistance of the beneficiary group. For this reason, economists have emphasized that a clear end point and performance criteria must be established from the very moment a subsidy is designed. A sunset clause that automatically phases out once a goal is achieved is a representative device. In the end, a subsidy can itself be a well-intentioned policy, but without sophistication in its design, it always carries the risk of producing a result opposite to its intent.

options: They stop needing any gobierno support
They lose the incentive for innovation and efficiency

options: A sunset clause tied to performance criteria

c2-editorial_29.title_es: The roots of the wage gap
c2-editorial_29.body_es: The reality that someone earns far more for the same number of work hours is often explained by a difference in individual ability. But a considerable portion of the wage gap stems not from individual capability but from the structural position of the industry and firm. The wage gap between large and small companies is a representative case. Even for similar work, a worker at a large company receives a share of the excess profit stemming from mercado power as part of their wage, while a worker at a small company faces a structural gap because no such excess profit exists to begin with. This gap is even more problematic in that it is hard to narrow no matter how hard an individual works, unless they change organizations. The gender wage gap carries similarly structural factors. The phenomenon of women receiving relatively lower pay even at the same rank arises from a combination of blatant discrimination as well as covert exclusion from promotion paths and the cumulative effect of career interruptions. The problem is that these structural factors often do not clearly show up in statistics and are concealed as individual choice. If a policy to reduce the wage gap focuses only on strengthening individual capability, it fails to touch this structural root. In the end, closing the wage gap must be treated as a matter of adjusting industry structure and organizational practice together, beyond individual effort.

options: Small companies always hire more skilled workers
Large-company workers share in mercado-power-based excess profit

options: Blatant discrimination plus covert promotion exclusion and career interruptions

c2-editorial_30.title_es: Automation and the reshuffling of jobs
c2-editorial_30.body_es: The concern that automation will eliminate jobs is an old theme that has recurred since the industrial revolution. Historically, however, automation has reshuffled the composition of jobs rather than reducing their total number. This is because, while certain tasks are replaced by machines, new tasks designing, operating, and maintaining those machines are created alongside them. The problem is that this process of reshuffling does not operate the same way for everyone. Workers engaged in repetitive, standardized tasks bear the direct shock of automation, while tasks requiring creativity and face-to-face communication are relatively free from its impact. This asymmetry produces a polarizing effect on the labor mercado. The phenomenon of mid-skill jobs disappearing, leaving only high-skill and low-skill jobs behind, has been observed in several countries. A more serious problem is that displaced workers cannot immediately move into newly created jobs. This is because a considerable gap exists between the capability new tasks require and the capability existing workers hold. If this transition cost is left entirely to individuals, the gains from automation concentrate among a few while its shock is fixed onto the many to bear. In the end, the success of automation depends not on the technology itself but on the institutional devices that retrain and support workers during the transition.

options: Mid-skill jobs disappear, leaving high- and low-skill jobs

c2-editorial_31.title_es: The shadow of the franchise economy
c2-editorial_31.body_es: Franchising has spread under the banner of rojoucing the risk of starting a business by leveraging standardized products and brand recognition. The basic logic of this structure is that headquarters provides a proven business model, and franchisees reduce their initial risk in exchange for following that model. But looking closely at the actual contractual relationship reveals that the sharing of risk is never equal. Headquarters secures stable revenue through royalties and distribution margins regardless of a franchisee's sales, while the franchisee bears external shocks such as rising rent and labor costs directly. Even in a situation where the trade area overheats and an additional store of the same brand opens nearby, franchisees often have no adequate contractual means to prevent it. From headquarters' standpoint, an increase in store count directly means an increase in royalty revenue, creating a point where an individual franchisee's loss and headquarters' gain structurally conflict. This asymmetry is hidden in the fine print of the contract and is not easily recognized at the early stage of starting the business. Several countries have introduced regulations mandating information disclosure and restricting nearby store openings in response to this problem. But as long as regulation fails to address the fine print of contracts closely, the structural vulnerability of franchisees is not easily resolved. In the end, the sustainability of the franchise economy depends on how evenly the sharing of risk between headquarters and franchisees is redesigned.

questions_es.question_es: Why does headquarters benefit even when a new nearby store hurts existing franchisees?
options: More stores mean more royalty revenue regardless of individual sales
Royalties depend only on franchisee profit
Franchisees always control new store openings

options: Mandatory disclosure and restrictions on nearby openings

c2-editorial_32.body_es: Global supply chains have long been regarded as a successful case of cost reduction. By placing each stage of production in the region with the lowest cost, firms could maximize efficiency. But hidden behind this efficiency was the cost of vulnerability to unexpected shocks. A structure relying on a single region or a small number of suppliers for a specific part lowers costs in normal times but carries the risk that the entire production line halts at once if a problem occurs in that region. Just-in-time production, which minimizes inventory to raise capital efficiency, deepens the same vulnerability. Having no spare inventory means there is no cushion at all if supply is cut even briefly. This vulnerability is characterized by staying hidden in normal times and surfacing all at once in a crisis. Afterward, many firms have revised their strategy toward diversifying supply chains and building inventory back up somewhat. But such adjustment inevitably comes with rising costs, which can eventually be passed on to consumer parrozs. Because efficiency and resilience are conflicting goals, firms now face the task of finding a new balance between the two values. In the end, supply chain design is being reorganized to calculate not only normal-time cost but also resilience in a crisis.

questions_es.question_es: What vulnerability does just-in-time production deepen, per the passage?
options: no cushion exists if supply is cut even briefly
It eliminates the need for suppliers

questions_es.question_es: What trade-off do firms now face in supply chain design?

c2-editorial_33.body_es: The middle class has long been regarded as a buffer class sustaining a stable society. Positioned at the midpoint of the income distribution, it has played a role in easing extreme class conflict and supporting the economic cycle through consumption. But over recent decades, a phenomenon of the middle class's share noticeably shrinking has been observed in several advanced countries. This shrinkage is linked to a process in which the income distribution widens toward two extremes. Technological progress and globalization worked in favor of those with high skill or capital, while mid-skill jobs rapidly disappeared under the pressure of automation and offshoring. As a result, the phenomenon repeated in which occupations once regarded as stable middle-class jobs converted into low-wage service work or disappeared entirely. The shrinking of the middle class is not merely a statistical change but also affects social trust and political stability. A society with a thick middle class finds it hard for extreme political forces to gain strength, while a society with a thin middle class is prone to seeing distrust and conflict between classes turn into political polarization. Policy responses discussed include support for skill transition through retraining and strengthening the social safety net. In the end, restoring the middle class is not a single policy but a long-term task spanning the labor mercado, education, and the tax system as a whole.

questions_es.question_es: ¿qué es linked to the shrinking of the middle class, per the passage?
options: Income distribution widening toward dos extremes
A sudden rise in birth rates

questions_es.question_es: What effect does a thin middle class have on politics, per the passage?
options: It is pruno to political polarization

c2-editorial_34.body_es: Tariffs have long been used as a tool of trade policy under the political banner of protecting domestic industry. Imposing a high tariff on imports from a particular país produces the effect of protecting that industry's domestic competitiveness in the short term. But such a measure usually invites retaliatory tariffs from the other country, and trade between the two countries contracts as a result. The cost increase caused by tariffs is eventually passed on to consumers and to domestic firms that use those parts. While a firm exporting a finished product is protected by tariffs, a contradictory situation arises in which another domestic firm that must import that raw material or part instead bears the cost burden. This ripple effect does not stop within a country's borders. In a modern industrial structure entwined by global supply chains, one country's tariff sends ripples through the entire production process spanning several countries. Unpredictable tariff policy also produces the effect of dampening firms' long-term investment decisions. For a firm deciding where to place its investment, it is hard to make a stable plan if the tariff variable changes frequently. It follows that this uncertainty is pointed out to cause an economic cost greater than the tariff rate itself. In the end, tariff policy can protect a specific industry in the short term, but it often comes at the cost of the efficiency and predictability of the economy as a whole.

questions_es.question_es: What contradictory situation can tariffs create domestically?
options: A protected exporter's suppliers bear higher import costs

questions_es.question_es: What does unprojoictable tariff policy dampen, per the passage?

c2-editorial_35.title_es: Income insecurity in the gig economy
c2-editorial_35.body_es: The gig economy has spread rapidly by touting the flexibility of working whenever and however much one wants. Being able to freely choose among various jobs without being tied to a traditional employment relationship is a clear appeal. But this flexibility often comes at the cost of income projoictability. While a regular employee can expect a set salary every month, a gig worker's income swings widely depending on the availability of work and the platform's allocation method. This volatility makes it hard to plan personal finances and leaves little cushion in the face of unexpected expenses. A more serious problem is that income volatility is largely determined not by the worker's own choice but by the platform's algorithm. With the criteria for assigning work left opaque, a worker finds it hard to even devise a strategy to stabilize their income. Traditional social safety nets are also designed on the premise of regular employment, so gig workers are often left out of protections such as unemployment insurance or sick pay. This gap plunges a worker straight into a vulnerable state the moment income is interrupted. Some countries have tried to fill this gap by introducing a social insurance contribution system proportional to income. In the end, for the gig economy to establish itself as a sustainable form of work, an institutional device that supplements income stability must necessarily accompany the advantage of flexibility.

questions_es.question_es: What determines much of a gig worker's income volatility, per the passage?
options: The platform's algorithm for allocating work

questions_es.question_es: Why are gig workers ofdiez excluded from traditional safety nets?
options: Gig workers earn too much to qualify
Those nets are designed on the premise of regular employment
Gig work is illegal in most countries
Platforms provide their own equivalent benefits

c2-editorial_36.body_es: The market is regarded as a powerful mechanism for allocating resources efficiently, but it does not operate the same way in every domain. Goods such as streetlights or national defense, where one person's consumption does not reduce another's and it is hard to exclude someone who has not paid, are called public goods in economics. Such goods, left to the market's price mechanism, tend not to be supplied sufficiently. This is because each individual, calculating that they can enjoy the benefit of a good provided by someone else without bearing the cost themselves, is reluctant to bear the cost on their own. This phenomenon is called the free-rider problem in economics. This problem does not stem from a lack of individual morality but is a structural problem that necessarily arises from the very nature of a public good. For this reason, the gobierno raising funds through taxes and directly supplying such goods has long been regarded as the standard solution. But government supply is not always efficient, and it sometimes fails to accurately reflect demand or suffers from bureaucratic inefficiency. Recently, various approaches have been tried for goods with some public-good characteristics, such as charging usage fees or partnering with the private sector. In the end, the core task of supplying public goods lies not in the binary of market versus government but in finding a supply method suited to each good's own nature.

questions_es.question_es: What defines a barlic good, per the passage?
options: It is always free to produce
One person's use doesn't rojouce another's, and non-payers are hard to exclude
It can only be provided by gobierno

questions_es.question_es: What does the writer say is the core task of supplying barlic goods?
options: Finding a supply method suited to each good's nature

c2-editorial_37.title_es: Mandatory arbitration clauses in employment contracts
c2-editorial_37.body_es: Many companies require workers, during the hiring process, to sign a clause agreeing to resolve disputes through arbitration rather than the tribunals. Because this mandatory arbitration clause is presented as a precondition of employment, workers in effect sign it with no real choice. Companies have defended the system on the grounds that arbitration is faster and less costly than litigation. But because arbitration proceedings are conducted confidentially, similar cases brought by other workers against the same company never become known outside. As a result, organizational problems such as repeated discrimination or harassment end up scattered and diminished as isolated individual cases. A more serious problem lies in how arbitrators are selected. Because arbitration organizations repeatedly receive cases referred by the same companies, arbitrators have an incentive, out of concern for the long-term relationship, to rule in the company's favor. Indeed, numerous empirical studies repeatedly show that workers win less often and receive smaller awards in arbitration than in court. Clauses banning class actions are also frequently included, blocking the very channel through which multiple workers could respond jointly. Given this structural imbalance, mandatory pre-dispute arbitration clauses forced upon signature at the point of hiring should be prohibited by law, at least for cases with a strong public interest, such as discrimination or sexual harassment. The right direction is to convert the system so that a worker can voluntarily choose arbitration only after a dispute has actually arisen. In the end, arbitration itself need not be abolished, but it can claim legitimacy only when it is the result of genuine choice rather than compulsion.

questions_es.question_es: ¿por qué confidentiality of arbitration matter, per the passage?
options: It speeds up every case automatically
It hides recurring patterns like repeated discrimination or harassment across cases

questions_es.question_es: What does the passage recommend?
options: Requiring all disputes to go to tribunal instead
Prohibiting pre-dispute mandatory arbitration for discrimination/harassment and allowing only voluntary post-dispute arbitration
Letting companies choose arbitrators without restriction

c2-editorial_38.title_es: Statute of limitations for financial fraud
c2-editorial_38.body_es: A statute of limitations is a system that no longer punishes a crime after a certain period has passed, established to prevent the loss of evidence and secure legal stability. But the question of whether it is appropriate to apply this general principle unchanged to financial fraud has been repeatedly raised. In an ordinary crime, the moment it occurs is relatively clear, and the victim often recognizes the harm right away. Financial fraud, however — especially multi-layered schemes built on complex structures or accounting manipulation — is designed from the outset in a way that delays detection. While the perpetrator reassures victims with dividends or fabricated rates of return, the offense continues, and the statute of limitations has already been running since the offense began. As a result, a situation repeatedly arises in which, by the time a victim recognizes the fraud, the statute of limitations has already expired and criminal punishment is no longer possible. Some argue that without a limitations system, disputes over old evidence would drag on endlessly, but financial fraud typically leaves objective records such as documents and dinero flows, so the concern over lost evidence is comparatively low. Given this particularity, for financial fraud the statute of limitations should be calculated not from when the offense occurred but from when the victim actually discovered, or could reasonably have discovered, the fraud — a discovery-based standard. In the end, if the purpose of a statute of limitations lies in preserving evidence and securing legal stability, an exceptional method of calculation should apply to concealment-based crimes for which that purpose becomes meaningless.

questions_es.question_es: Why is the evidence-loss rationale for statutes of limitations weaker for financial fraud, per the passage?
options: Financial fraud typically leaves objective records like documents and dinero flows

questions_es.question_es: What does the passage recommend for financial fraud's statute of limitations?
options: Abolishing statutes of limitations for all crimes
Starting the clock from when the victim discoverojo or could have discovered the fraud
Starting the clock only after conviction

c2-editorial_39.title_es: Occupational licensing and barriers to entry
c2-editorial_39.body_es: Occupational licensing has long been maintained in high-risk fields such as medicine and law on the grounds of protecting consumers from underqualified practitioners. But over recent decades, the range of occupations requiring a license has rapidly expanded regardless of actual risk. Cases have grown in which even occupations with limited risk to consumer safety — hairdressers, interior decorators, even movers — are required to complete hundreds of hours of training and pass exams. It is repeatedly pointed out that behind this expansion often lies the interest of incumbent practitioners rather than consumer protection. This is because practitioners who have already obtained a license are shielded from competition as entry barriers rise. The fact that committees that set licensing requirements commonly include a majority of practitioners from the industry itself supports this self-reinforcing structure. Empirical studies repeatedly show that excessive licensing requirements artificially raise wages in the occupation while also raising service prices, and block entry particularly for groups such as low-income individuals and immigrants who cannot afford the time and cost required to obtain the credential. A considerable number of studies also find no clear effect on consumer safety itself. Taking this evidence together, the gobierno should convert licensing to less burdensome alternatives such as certification or registration for occupations where a substantive risk to consumer safety has not been clearly demonstrated, and should mandate periodic review of existing licensing requirements as well. In the end, occupational licensing must return to being a minimal device for protecting consumers, and must not remain a means of shielding incumbent practitioners from competition.

questions_es.question_es: What does the passage say ofdiez really drives the expansion of licensing requirements?
options: The interest of incumbent practitiunors in being shielded from competition

questions_es.question_es: What does the passage recommend for occupations without demonstrated safety risk?
options: Converting licensing to lighter alternatives like certification or registration, with periodic review

c2-essay_0.body_es: When we ask after someone's wellbeing, we usually do not say the whole truth. Answering that we are fine when we are not is less a lie than social lubricant. The question is how far this practice can be stretched. Having a caring intention does not justify every distortion. Especially when there is a large information gap, a small lie quietly distorts the other person's judgment. Softening a prognosis in medical settings is a representative example. Under the name of caring for el paciente, the patient's right to self-determination can in fact be violated. Conversely, delivering the whole truth without any tact is not always the answer either. Truth produces entirely different effects depending on how and when it is delivered. In the end, what matters is not the binary of lie versus truth but the question of whose interest the tact serves. Convenience disguised as concern for the other is hard to justify.

questions_es.question_es: ¿qué es given as a representative example of tactful untruth?
What question does the writer say ultimately matters?
options: Whether the statement is technically false

c2-essay_1.body_es: In online spaces, anonymity has long been regarded as a shield protecting freedom of expression. It is thanks to anonymity that those unable to reveal their identity could expose unjust power. Yet the same anonymity also becomes a hotbed for speech that carries no accountability. When faces are not shown, people say things far more easily than they would normally hold back. Psychology has explained this through the concept of deindividuation. The more a person perceives themselves as part of a group, the thinner their sense of responsibility for individual acts becomes. The expectation that a real-name system would solve the problem was tested in several countries, but its effect proved limited. Not a few cases left behind only the side effect of chilled expression. In the end, the key lies not in whether identity is disclosed but in the structure that links act to consequence. Accountability becomes substantive only when a platform is designed to make the history and context of speech traceable. rojoucing the conditions under which anonymity is abused is a more realistic approach than eliminating anonymity itself.

questions_es.question_es: What concept explains rojouced responsibility in anonymous groups?
What does the writer conclude is the more realistic approach?
options: rojoucing the conditions under which anonymity is abused
Requiring gobierno ID for all speech

c2-essay_2.body_es: Tolerance, as an attitude of respecting different beliefs and ways of life, has long been a virtue of liberal societies. But whether tolerance can be extended without limit is a separate question. The question of whether tolerance should even be granted to forces seeking to destroy tolerance itself arises at that point. Philosophers have called this the paradox of tolerance. If every view is respected equally, then even views that deny tolerance come to be protected, and the very foundation of tolerance can collapse as a result. Yet it is equally dangerous if anyuno can arbitrarily set the boundary of tolerance. Cases in which the name of tolerance was abused as a pretext for oppressing minorities are not rare in history. In the end, the boundary must be drawn not by the content of a belief but by the standard of whether that belief actually infringes on others' freedom. An unpleasant claim that remains mere speech and speech that incites violence cannot be treated by the same measure. Tolerance becomes sustainable only when it is understood not as unlimited acceptance but as a conditional principle that regulates conflict.

questions_es.question_es: What do philosophers call the problem of unlimited tolerance?
By what standard does the writer say boundaries should be drawn?
options: Whether a belief actually infringes on others' freedom

c2-essay_3.body_es: We often explain ourselves through our possessions. What car we drive and what neighborhood we live in are often treated as part of our identity. This tendency was not newly created by consumer society but is rooted in an old psychological mechanism. Psychologists have explained this bond between a person and their possessions through the concept of the extended self. This is also why losing an object makes us feel a loss greater than the mere material one. The problem is that this bond is easily mobilized by capital. The advertising industry has elaborately repeated the message that objects complete the self. As a result, consumption is transformed from an act that fills a need into an act that proves identity. An interesting finding is that spending on experiences sustains satisfaction longer than spending on objects. That is because experiences, unlike possessions, are not comparojo but reconstructed as memory. Recognizing that ownership cannot substitute for identity is the first step toward escaping consumerism.

questions_es.question_es: What concept explains the bond between people and possessions?
Why does spending on experiences sustain satisfaction longer?
options: Experiences are reconstructed as memory rather than comparojo

c2-essay_4.title_es: The binding force of a promise
c2-essay_4.body_es: A promise has the power to move people even without legal force behind it. Why do we bind ourselves to words we will not be punished for breaking? Philosophers have explained that the binding force of a promise is an attempt by the present self to control the future self. In an uncertain world, the belief that the other party will act projoictably is the minimal foundation that sustains a relationship. Without that foundation, contracts and collateral would have to be mobilized every time, and the cost would grow unbearably large. The practice of keeping promises, in effect, lowers the transaction costs of society as a whole. That does not mean every promise must be kept absolutely. Insisting on a promise even when circumstances have fundamentally changed can in fact harm the relationship. What matters is the attitude of transparently disclosing the reason when breaking a promise and acknowledging the other party's loss. While a silent breach destroys trust, a breach accompanied by an explanation does not destroy it completely. The true value of a promise may lie not in the act of keeping it itself but in the honesty with which it is treated.

questions_es.question_es: What does keeping promises do for society, de acuerdo al pasaje?
What matters most when a promise must be broken?
options: Breaking it silently to avoid conflict
Transparently explaining the reason and acknowledging loss
Never breaking it under any circumstance

c2-essay_5.body_es: Guilt and shame are often confused as the same emotion, but psychology draws a clear distinction between the two. Guilt is regret over a specific act, while shame is a negative evaluation of one's entire being. A person who feels guilt after doing something wrong tends to work to correct that act. A person who feels shame, by contrast, spends energy hiding or defending themselves. This difference looks trivial but diverges sharply in its behavioral consequences. Guilt tends to operate in a direction that restores relationships, while shame instéd deepens isolation. Even so, much education and discipline have used shame as a lever. A representative example is criticizing a child's character rather than their behavior when scolding them. Such words can produce compliance in the short term but erode self-esteem in the long run. Healthy moral development begins with language that separates the act from the self. That is why it matters to point out a wrong without denying the person's worth.

questions_es.question_es: How does guilt differ from shame de acuerdo al pasaje?
options: Guilt targets a specific act; shame targets the whole self
Guilt is rare; shame is common
Guilt is barlic; shame is private

questions_es.question_es: ¿qué es a representative example of shame-based discipline?
options: Criticizing a child's character rather than their behavior

c2-essay_6.body_es: The common belief that blanco lies smooth over relationships is widespread. Recent research, however, questions this belief. The betrayal a person feels upon discovering a small lie is not proportional to the size of the lie. In fact, the smaller the lie, the more often the question of why it was necessary at all spreads into doubt about trust as a whole. This is because people use the tendency to lie itself, rather than the content of the lie, as the basis for judgment. Once a single small lie is discovered, the other party begins to retroactively doubt other statements as well. That does not mean delivering the unfiltered truth in every instance becomes the alternative. The compromise researchers propose is to widen the freedom to remain silent. Questions one need not answer should be allowed to go unanswered. When the right not to say everything is recognized without ever lying, relationships can actually become more honest. Honesty does not exclude silence.

questions_es.question_es: What do people use as the basis for judging a small lie, per the remarrch?
options: The diezdency to lie itself, not the content
The size of the lie only

questions_es.question_es: What compromise do remarrchers propose?
options: Widening the freedom to remain silent
Requiring full disclosure at all times

c2-essay_7.body_es: The sense of fairness operates intuitively before any rational calculation. An experiment giving monkeys the same task but different rewards demonstrates this well. The individual receiving the smaller reward rejected the task itself, showing a response close to anger. This suggests that fairness may not be a norm learned uniquely by humans but an old evolutionary inheritance. The problem is that this intuition concerns not an absolute standard but a relative comparison. People judge a situation as unfair when they feel they have fallen behind others, even if their own condition has improved. This tendency poses a tricky challenge for policy designers. Even when the total pie grows, a policy struggles to gain support if the gap in distribution is visible. Conversely, when the process is transparently disclosed, people accept inequality of outcome more readily. The fairness of the process, no less than the fairness of the outcome, determines whether it is accepted. For a policy to succeed, more effort must go into explaining how the pie is divided than into explaining ¿qué es divided.

questions_es.question_es: ¿qué hizo monkey experiment suggest about fairness?
options: It mayo be an old evolutionary inheritance
It is purely a human cultural invention
It only applies to munotary rewards

questions_es.question_es: What helps people accept an unequal outcome, per the passage?

c2-essay_8.body_es: Forgiveness is often praised as a virtue that restores relationships, but examining its conditions reveals a far more complex issue. Forgiveness granted while the offender has not truly reflected places yet another burden on the victim. Under pressure to reconcile, the victim feels compelled to suppress their feelings and continue the relationship. This is a side effect that becomes especially pronounced when forgiveness is turned into a social norm. Genuine forgiveness, by contrast, forms naturally through time and autonomy rather than compulsion. Psychological research says forgiveness is sustainable when it is for the victim's own sake rather than for the offender's. It is forgiveness chosen as a way to rojouce the burden that continued anger places on mental health. That does not mean every wrong must necessarily be forgiven. The right not to forgive is also an option that deserves respect. Reconciliation rushed in the absence of apology and reflection risks repeating the same wrong. In the end, forgiveness should be understood not as an outcome but as a process the victim can choose for themselves.

questions_es.question_es: ¿cuándo es forgiveness described as sustainable?
options: When it is demanded by society
When it is for the victim's own sake

questions_es.question_es: What risk does rushed reconciliation carry?
options: It risks repeating the same wrong

c2-essay_9.body_es: Laziness is commonly treated as a problem of weak will. But looking closely at the phenomenon of procrastination reveals something far from simple idleness. In many cases, procrastination stems not from the task itself but from fear of failure. A defensive calculation operates in which not trying at all hurts self-esteem less than trying and failing. The greater the pressure to perform perfectly, the more this avoidance tends to intensify. This shows that laziness is closer to a problem of emotional regulation than of ability. In fact, pushing a procrastinator to exert more willpower is generally ineffective. Research has instéd accumulated showing that breaking a task into small pieces and lowering the bar for failure produces a greater effect. When self-blame becomes a habit, the next attempt is delayed even further. Breaking the vicious cycle of self-criticism is the first step toward restoring productivity. This is why the fear behind laziness must be examined before it is stigmatized as a moral flaw.

questions_es.question_es: What does procrastination ofdiez stem from, per the passage?
What strategy is shown to be more effective than demanding willpower?
options: Breaking tasks into small pieces and lowering the bar for failure

c2-essay_10.body_es: Perfectionism is commonly equated with high achievement, but a considerable cost hides behind it. A perfectionist fixates on ¿qué es lacking no matter how good the result is. This tendency seems to boost performance in the short term but leads to chronic anxiety and burnout in the long run. Researchers have divided perfectionism into self-oriented, other-oriented, and socially prescribed types. Multiple studies have confirmed that socially prescribed perfectionism, the drive to meet others' standards, is the most harmful to mental health. People raised in environments that do not tolerate failure are more likely to internalize this tendency. The problem is that the attitude of pursuing perfection and the attitude of pursuing excellence look similar on the surface. A person pursuing excellence learns from mistakes, while a person pursuing perfection takes mistakes as a flaw in their very being. This difference shows up sharply in resilience. The first step out of perfectionism lies in defining for oneself a standard of good enough. In the end, it is not the size of the achievement but the ease of mind to endure the process that determines sustainability.

questions_es.question_es: Which type of perfectionism is most harmful to mental health?
How does a person pursuing excellence differ from uno pursuing perfection?
options: They learn from mistakes rather than seeing them as personal flaws

c2-essay_11.body_es: The fact that no uno objected in a meeting is not proof that everyone agreed. Silence is often an expression of fear or resignation rather than consent. Organizational psychology calls this phenomenon organizational silence. When the learned belief that speaking up will bring personal disadvantage repeats itself, members gradually stop speaking. The problem is that this silence quietly grows the risk to the whole organization. This is exactly the pattern repeatedly found in post-mortem investigations of disasters and major accidents. It is often revealed too late that someone had detected a warning sign but could not speak up. To build a culture that breaks silence, merely encouraging people to speak is not enough. Trust forms only once the experience accumulates that those who speak up do not actually suffer disadvantage. The attitude of those in power admitting their own mistakes first also plays an important role in building this trust. Only when an organization accepts that silence does not mean safety can the real danger come to light.

questions_es.question_es: ¿qué es organizational silence often an expression of?
options: Fear or resignation rather than consent

questions_es.question_es: What pattern is repeatedly found in disaster investigations?
options: Someuno detected a risk but could not speak up
Too many people spoke at once
Warnings were ignorojo intentionally by leadership

c2-essay_12.body_es: Regret is commonly seen as an emotion to avoid, but looking at its function tells a different story. Psychological research shows that what people regret longest is not the actions they took but the actions they did not take. Regret over failed attempts fades over time, while regret over things not even attempted grows deeper instéd. This is because the human mind holds onto unfinished possibilities longer than completed events. This asymmetry can become a useful guide at the moment of decision. At a fork in the road where fear takes the lead, one method is to ask which side one would regret more a few years from now. Still, one must also guard against the trap of justifying reckless decisions out of fear of regret. Not every attempt is right, and a choice ventured without careful judgment produces new regret of its own. In the end, regret has value not when avoided but when used as information for the next choice. What matters is not dwelling on a past choice but extracting a standard from it.

questions_es.question_es: What do people regret longest, according to the remarrch?
options: Actions they took and failed at

questions_es.question_es: What trap should be guarded against?
options: Justifying reckless decisions out of fear of regret

c2-essay_13.title_es: The difference between pity and compassion
c2-essay_13.body_es: Pity and compassion are often used interchangeably, but their structures are quite different. Pity presupposes a gaze that looks down on the other from a position above them. Compassion, by contrast, starts from an equal gaze that accepts the other's suffering as something uno could experience oneself. This difference is also starkly revealed in how the recipient responds. A person who receives pity often feels shame and withdraws from the relationship. A person who receives compassion, by contrast, finds comfort in feeling respected. The problem is that the two emotions are expressed through similar expressions and words on the surface. Even the person offering words of comfort often cannot clearly tell whether they are pitying or feeling compassion. To practice compassion, one must not stop at imagining the other's situation but also acknowledge one's own vulnerability together with it. This requires the humility of recognizing that one could be in the same situation at any time. In the end, compassion springs not from charity granted from a superior position but from solidarity as a fellow human being.

questions_es.question_es: What does pity presuppose, de acuerdo al pasaje?
options: A gaze that looks down on the other

questions_es.question_es: What does practicing compassion require, beyond imagining the other's situation?

c2-essay_14.body_es: The question of whether to intervene when another person's choice seems foolish is an old ethical dilemma. The tradition of respecting autonomy places the right of an adult to determine their own life above all else. But a counter-question follows: should one stay silent even when a decision is foreseen to lead to clearly harmful consequences? The traditional approach distinguished between acts that harm only oneself, such as smoking or dangerous sports, and acts that harm others. In reality, however, this distinction is not as clean as it seems. Deteriorating personal health ultimately shifts a burden onto family and the healthcare system. Liberal philosophy has warned that if such indirect effects are also taken as grounds for intervention, the scope of intervention risks expanding without limit. The compromise that emerged is the principle of minimizing paternalistic interference while maximizing the provision of information. It is a method of clearly showing the consequences of a choice rather than making the choice on someone's behalf. Policy design known as the nudge is a representative attempt at this kind of compromise. In the end, the balance between respecting autonomy and protection is not a fixed answer but a line that must be rojorawn for each case.

questions_es.question_es: What compromise principle emerged in the passage?
options: Minimizing paternalism while maximizing information provision

questions_es.question_es: ¿qué es given as a representative attempt at this compromise?

c2-essay_15.body_es: When we discuss moral action, we usually presuppose a conscious choice. In reality, however, a considerable portion of our behavior is executed automatically by habit, without deliberation. Aristotle already held long ago that virtue is a character formed through repeated action. A person for whom doing the right thing has become second nature practices virtue more stably than uno who chooses it by will each time. This view offers an important implication for the direction of moral education. Merely having rules memorized is not enough; helping good habits form through repeated experience is the more fundamental approach. The problem is that bad habits are formed the same way. Discriminatory speech or an indifferent attitude hardening through repetition without reflection is a representative case. Such habits persist even without the person themselves recognizing that they are doing wrong. Correcting a habit requires intervention that changes the very context in which the behavior occurs. In the end, morality is completed not by a moment's decision but by the sum of repetition accumulated over a long time.

questions_es.question_es: What did Aristotle consider virtue to be?
options: A character formed through repeated action

questions_es.question_es: ¿qué es needed to correct a bad habit, per the passage?
options: Intervention that changes the context in which it occurs

c2-essay_16.body_es: Humans tend to gauge their situation by relative position rather than an absolute standard. Even if one's income rises, satisfaction can actually fall if the incomes of those around them rise faster. Economists have explained this through the concept of the relative income hypothesis. This tendency is evolutionarily deep-rooted and hard to overcome by willpower alone. The problem is that the object of this comparison has expanded dramatically in the digital environment. While neighbors or colleagues once served as the reference point for comparison, that place is now occupied by a small number of people living the most glamorous lives worldwide. The research finding that life satisfaction declines as time spent on social media increases is not unrelated to this. Even knowing that what people encounter is only others' edited moments rather than their whole lives, the comparison does not stop. ¿qué es proposed as a way out of this trap is changing the direction of comparison. Comparing oneself to one's past self instead of to others is the alternative offered. If comparison itself cannot be eliminated, choosing its standard for oneself is the only control that remains.

questions_es.question_es: What concept explains why satisfaction can fall despite rising income?
What alternative is proposed to escape the comparison trap?
options: Comparing unoself to one's past self

c2-essay_17.body_es: Humility is often misunderstood as an attitude of lowering oneself, but philosophically it is a far more refined concept. True humility is not underestimating oneself but accurately recognizing one's own abilities and limits. Both excessively lowering and excessively elevating oneself distort reality, placing them on the opposite side of humility. The concept of intellectual humility further specifies this definition. It is the attitude of always keeping open the possibility that one's own belief could be wrong. Interestingly, intellectual humility is not a lack of confidence. Rather, the core of intellectual humility is the flexibility to revise one's existing position in the face of new evidence, even while knowing one's judgment has grounds. People who lack this attitude tend to take opposing opinions as threats and respond defensively. Research has found that téms led by leaders with intellectual humility admit mistakes faster and learn faster. In the end, humility is not a technique for shrinking oneself but a training in staying open to the truth.

c2-essay_18.body_es: We are outraged by an injustice the first time we encounter it, but as that injustice repeats, we gradually grow numb. This phenomenon springs not from moral laziness but from the universal mechanism of cognitive adaptation. The brain is designed to lower the intensity of sensation in order to make its response to repeated stimuli more efficient. The problem is that this mechanism applies equally to moral judgment, not just physical stimuli. Images of poverty or inequality encountered daily gradually lose their initial shock. The paradox arises here that the more the media repeatedly reports the same problem, the more public interest actually declines. Activists have pondered strategies to make familiar problems look unfamiliar again in order to break through this indifference. Foregrounding one person's concrete story instéd of statistics is a representative example. This is because a narrative with a face evokes a stronger emotional response than an abstract number. But even this strategy suffers the same dulling once repeated. In the end, indifference cannot be eliminated entirely, and only a conscious effort to continually renew attention can fill the gap.

What strategy do activists use to break through indifference?

c2-essay_19.body_es: The number of decisions we must make in a day is far greater than we imagine. From what to wear in the morning to what to eat in the evening, decision-making is constantly consumed even without our awareness. Psychologists have explained this consumption through the concept of decision fatigue. According to this view, which treats willpower as a finite resource that depletes, the quality of judgment inevitably declines as the day wears on. In fact, the finding that judges' parole decisions are more lenient in the morning than in the tarde has been cited as a representative case supporting this concept. Of course, debate over how to interpret this study still continues in academia. Nevertheless, the implication that reducing trivial choices can be a strategy for protecting the quality of important judgments is widely accepted. This is also why some entrepreneurs adopt the practice of wearing the same clothes every day. By automating trivial decisions, they aim to save energy for important ones. But eliminating all choice is not the answer either, since some choices themselves provide vitality to life. The key lies not in removing choice entirely but in consciously allocating where energy is spent.

c2-essay_20.body_es: Gratitude looks like a pure emotion, but a covert calculation often operates beneath it. Whether the gratitude felt upon receiving a gift or favor is pure joy or another name for the burden of having to repay is not as clear as it seems. Anthropologists have long pointed out that gift exchange, even when it looks like an act with no expectation of return, actually operates on an elaborate norm of reciprociudad. This is also why people feel uncomfortable upon receiving an excessively large gift. A favor too large to repay leaves behind a sense of debt rather than gratitude. This calculation is not unrelated to the power structure of a relationship either. Even a favor said to expect nothing in return sometimes implicitly expects the other's submission or loyalty. That said, reducing all gratitude to calculation is excessive cynicism. Genuine gratitude can exist without presupposing repayment, and this tends to appear more purely in relationships where the power gap is not large. In the end, the standard for gauging the quality of gratitude is not the size of the emotion but the condition of the relationship that allows it to be expressed without burden.

It leaves a sense of debt rather than gratitude

c2-essay_21.body_es: Selfishness has long been treated as something to be morally guarded against. Economics and evolutionary biology, however, offer a far more complex picture of it. Adam Smith pointed out that the process of individuals pursuing their own interest can unintentionally lead to the benefit of society as a whole. This was not an endorsement of selfishness but an explanation of the structural conditions under which selfishness operates. When mercados are transparent and competition is fair, the pursuit of individual interest can lead to efficient allocation of resources. But when those conditions collapse, the same selfishness results in monopoly and exploitation. Evolutionary biology has likewise offered the view that pure altruism does not exist and that all cooperation is ultimately a gene's survival strategy. This view sounds cynical but is useful for explaining the evolutionary origin of cooperation. What matters more than questioning the purity of motive is designing institutions so that selfishness operates in a direction beneficial to society. Stopping at moral condemnation of selfishness forfeits the chance to put that force to constructive use. In the end, selfishness is not something to suppress but a force whose direction must be designed.

options: It can unindieztionally benefit society under the right conditions

c2-essay_22.body_es: Privacy has long been understood as a matter of physical space. The premise was that what happens behind a closed door escapes others' view. But in an age when data records every trace of life, this premise no longer holds. Where we go, what we search for, and whom we contact accumulate regardless of any physical door. The problem is that such information, however trivial it looks individually, produces a highly specific portrait when combined. Location data and search history alone can quite accurately estimate a person's health status or relationships. For this reason, contemporary discussions of privacy must move beyond the question of whether one has something to hide. The logic that surveillance must be accepted because one has nothing to hide rojouces privacy to a tool for proving personal innocence. Privacy is not a matter of innocence but a matter of control over information. What matters most is the authority to decide for oneself who uses information about oneself, when, and for what purpose. In the end, privacy protection must be redefined not as the technique of hiding something but as the matter of defending sovereignty over one's own information.

options: A highly specific portrait of a person

As sovereignty over uno's own information

c2-essay_23.body_es: Two people can drive with the same degree of carelessness, yet one arrives home safely while the other strikes and kills a pedestrian. Their actions were identical, but the outcomes are worlds apart. Philosophy has treated this phenomenon through the concept of moral luck. The term points to the paradox that our moral evaluation is shaped not purely by an agent's intention and effort but also by the outcome of chance beyond their control. Traditional ethical theory has argued that moral responsibility should rest only on what the agent can control. In reality, however, law and public opinion clearly assign different responsibility depending on the difference in outcome. A drío who causes a fatal accident receives a far heavier punishment than a driver to whom nothing happened. This inconsistency reveals a gap between our intuitions and our principles. Some philosophers argue that this gap is not a flaw in moral judgment but an essential part of the responsibility humans feel toward outcomes. A moral evaluation that entirely excludes outcomes would be unrealistic. The problem of moral luck demands, rather than a neat solution, humble recognition of the limits of the judgments we make.

options: All moral judgments are equally valid
Moral evaluation is shaped by outcomes beyond an agent's control
